This is the first surah revealed to begin with a disjointed letter of the alphabet.

They wrote the letter (ن) in the form in which it is written in script, and it is the name of the letter, which is (nūn) (with a nūn after it, then a waw, then a nūn). Analogically, the three letters should have been written, because writing follows pronunciation, and what is pronounced is the name of the letter, not its form. For if you wish to write, for example, the word for "sword" (sayf), you write sīn, yā', fā', and you do not draw the shape of a sword.

It is read by the name of the letter, not by spelling it out, as already explained at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

It is pronounced as the name nūn with the final letter unvowelled (sukūn), like words in pause before governing particles enter upon them. Thus it is recited in the widely transmitted readings (al-qira'at al-mutawatira).

As for the pen sworn by, it has been said that it refers to what is alluded to by the pen, namely the connection of God's knowledge with the existing and future beings, or that it is an unseen existent known only to God. From Mujahid and Qatadah: it is the pen mentioned in His saying ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ [al-'Alaq: 4] ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 5]. I say: this is the one that fits His saying ﴿and what they inscribe﴾ outwardly, and it is what the situation of the polytheists addressed in the discourse requires, for they knew only the pen, which is the instrument of writing among the People of the Book and among those Arabs who knew writing.

Among the benefits of this oath is that this Qur'an is the book of Islam, and that it would be written and read among the Muslims. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to order his companions to write what was revealed to him. The definite article in "the pen" is the definite article of the genus.

And ﴿what they inscribe﴾ means the lines written with the pen, and "mā" may be a relative pronoun, meaning "what they write of the pages," or it may be a verbal-noun particle, meaning "and their inscribing in lines." It is also possible that it is an oath by the pens with which the scribes of the revelation wrote the Qur'an, so that ﴿what they inscribe﴾ is an oath by their writing, and thus an oath by the Qur'an, to affirm that the Qur'an is not the speech of a madman

as has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿By the clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3] in Surat al-Zukhruf. "Yasturun" is the present tense of sataran; it is said: sataru (from the pattern of nasara), when one writes several words from which rows of writing result. Its root is derived from al-satr, which is cutting, because the rows of writing appear as if they were pieces.

The pronoun in "yasturūn" refers to something not mentioned in the speech but known to the hearers, because the mention of the pen indicates scribes who write with it. So the wording of the oath is connected to the instrument of writing and to writing, and what is meant is the written thing, by the use of the verbal noun for the passive participle. It is thus like the passive verb, because the inscribers are not known, as if it were said: "and the inscribed," like His saying ﴿and a Book inscribed﴾ [al-Tur: 2] ﴿on parchment unrolled﴾ [al-Tur: 3].

As for one who interprets "the pen" as the connection of God's knowledge with what will be, he makes the pronoun in "yasturūn" refer to the angels, so that the inscribing is a symbol for the angels' execution of what God has commanded them to execute upon receiving it, that is, they write it down in order to act upon it or to convey it from some of them to others in a manner that admits no addition or reduction; this exactness is likened to a scribe's exact recording of what he wishes to convey without change.

The thing sworn to is the negation that the Prophet (ﷺ) is mad, and the address to him in this is a consolation for him, lest the statement of the polytheists, when he called them to Islam, "He is mad," should grieve him. That is what they said to the Prophet (ﷺ) face to face, and God related it about them at the end of the surah: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad."﴾ [al-Qalam: 51]. Likewise, every place in which the negation of the attribute of madness is mentioned about him is a refutation of the statements of the polytheists, like His saying ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22]. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) has slipped in this matter with a slip unworthy of his knowledge.

The purpose of negating madness from him is to affirm what the polytheists intended to deny, namely that he is a messenger from God, for when they denied him the quality of messengerhood, they put in its place the quality of madness. So when what they claimed is negated, what he claimed is established.

Their statement and their emphasis on it, with the particle "inna" and the lam of initiation, when they said ﴿Indeed, he is mad﴾ [al-Qalam: 51], has been answered with stronger emphases than theirs: it is sworn to, the particle "bi" which is added after a negation for its emphasis is used after the negation, and the nominal sentence is negated, since the nominal sentence indicates the stability of the predicate, that is, its realization. These are three emphases.

His saying ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾ was made in al-Kashshaf a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in "majnun" (mad), which is negated. The sense is: the description of madness is negated by the grace of your Lord upon you. The "bi" is for accompaniment or causation, that is, because of God's favour in that He cleared you of defects. What I see is that it is a parenthetical clause, and that the "bi" is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, its estimate being: that this is by the grace of your Lord, in the manner that has been said about the connection of the "bi" in His saying "in the name of God," and this is what their usage requires, like the saying of the Hamasi poet al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas al-Lahabi:

"Each has an intention to hate his companion: by the grace of God, we bring you and you bring us..."

Ibn al-Hajib in his Amali held that "by the grace of your Lord" is connected to what the negative particle "ma" contains of the meaning of a verb, and he estimated it as: "It is negated that you be mad by the grace of your Lord." When God strengthened His Messenger (ﷺ) and repelled the slander of his enemies, He followed this with honouring him with a great reward for the harm he suffered from the polytheists, in His saying ﴿And indeed for you is a reward never cut off﴾, given the context of its occurrence after His saying ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman,﴾ emphasising this with the particle "inna," the lam of initiation, and the fronting of the prepositional phrase, which is in His saying "for you" (lak).

By this the meaning of establishment that the particle of elevation conveys in His saying ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾ becomes clearer: he is firmly established in it, the magnificent character within himself, and firmly established in it in his religious call.

Know that the sum of the great character, which is the highest of good character, is: religious devotion (tadayyun), knowledge of realities (ma'rifat al-haqa'iq), forbearance of the soul (hilm al-nafs), justice, patience in hardships, acknowledging the one who does good, humility, asceticism (zuhd), chastity (iffa), forgiveness, steadfastness (al-jumud, firmness in what is right), modesty (haya'), courage, good silence, deliberateness (ta'uddah), dignity (waqar), mercy, and good dealing and good companionship.

Character traits are hidden within the soul, and their manifestations are the conduct of their possessor in his speech, the brightness of his face, his steadfastness, his judgment, his movement and stillness, his food and drink, the discipline he gives his family, the one who looks upon him, and what follows from that of his esteem among people, the goodness of the praise given to him, and his reputation.

As for their manifestations in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they are in all of that, and in his governance of his community, and in what was specially granted to him of eloquence of speech and comprehensive brevity of expression.

[Page 66]

﴿So you will see and they will see,﴾ ﴿which of you is the afflicted one.﴾

The *fa'* here is *li-l-tafri'* (resultative, marking a consequence) of His statement ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ (al-Qalam: 2), in view of what His statement ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾ (al-Qalam: 2) implies of refuting a claim made about him, which his enemies in the religion had uttered. He began by refuting their slander, and then made it a consequence that when they look at the proofs and observe the characteristics, they will know which of the two groups is the afflicted one. Are they afflicted by turning away from the truth and right guidance, or is he afflicted in his intellect, as they fabricated?

The intended meaning is what is in His statement "they will see," but His statement "you will see" was incorporated into it so that mentioning both sides would allow the formulation of an even-handed statement (i.e., one calling to fairness), in the manner of His statement ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ (Saba': 24), because the Qur'an reaches their ears and is recited to them.

The two verbs ﴿tubsiru﴾ and ﴿yubsiruna﴾ are in the sense of physical sight (*al-basar al-hissi*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is "you will know and they will know," so he treated it like the use of the verb of seeing in the sense of supposing (*al-zann*). Perhaps he intended to explain the resulting meaning, since it has been said that the verb derived from *abṣara* is not used in the sense of supposing or believing according to the majority of lexicographers and grammarians, contrary to Hisham, as stated in *al-Tashil*. So the meaning is: you will see and they will see with the sight of the eye which of you is the afflicted one. If it means knowledge, then the Prophet (ﷺ) indeed saw that. The *sin* in "fasatubsiru" is for emphasis (*li-l-ta'kid*). As for the polytheists, they will see that, i.e., they will know the traces of their afflictions, and that is in what they see on the Day of Badr and the Day of the Conquest.

If it means physical sight, then the *sin* and the *ta'* in both verbs are for the future (*li-l-istiqbal*).

The pronoun in "yubsiruna" refers to a known referent supposed in the mind of the hearer, namely the polytheists who say: he is a madman.

*Ayy* is an ambiguous noun (*ism mubham*) which becomes definite by what is added to it. It appears that the referent of *ayy* is an individual or a group distinguished from a partner in its group by a genus or attribute, with a real or stipulated distinguishing feature. This is the referent of *ayy* in all its positions. It has many uses in speech: it may take the sense of the relative pronoun, the sense of the conditional, the sense of interrogation, the sense of drawing attention to a perfect exemplar (*al-tanwih bi-kamil*), and the sense of the definite with *al-* when it is joined to its vocative. In all of these it conveys something distinguished from what shares with it in the group signified by what is added to it. So His statement ﴿which of you is the afflicted one﴾ means: which man, or which group among you, is the afflicted one. *Ayy* here is a noun in the position of the object of ﴿you will see and they will see﴾, or related to it in the manner of a prepositional object.

The use of *ayy* in interrogation was previously mentioned at His statement ﴿then in what statement after this will they believe﴾ (al-A'raf: 185) in Surat al-A'raf.

*Al-maftun* is a passive participle (*ism maf'ul*), meaning one who has been struck by a *fitnah* (trial, affliction). It may be meant as madness, since madness is counted in Arabic speech among afflictions; they say of the madman: "the jinn have afflicted him" (*fatanathu al-jinn*). It may also be meant as what applies to one whose affair is disturbed and whose intellect is afflicted with bewilderment and instability. The word is chosen here instead of *majnun*, in a speech that is directed or equivocal (*al-kalam al-muwajjah aw al-tawriyah*), so that it can be applied to both sides.

If some of the polytheists were not like the madmen who rush to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) without insight, they were in the affliction of the disorder of his statements and actions, like Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their like, who incited the common people to slander the Prophet (ﷺ) with various contradictory statements.

On this view, the *ba'* is extra (*zā'idah*) to emphasise the connection of the verb with its object; the original is "ayyukum al-maftun," so it is like the *ba'* in His statement ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 6). It may also be that the *ba'* is for place (*zarfiyyah*). The meaning: in which of the two groups among you is the madman found, i.e., who truly fits this description. This becomes an allusion (*ta'rid*) against Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and others among the instigators of evil over the mob of Quraysh, with these statements resembling those of madmen. That is because they described a man known among the sensible, mentioned for soundness of intellect and trustworthiness in the pre-Islamic period, and they described him as a madman. They were like one who claims that the day is night, or who describes an extremely cold day as hot. So this one is likened to a madman, and for this reason *al-maftun* in the verse is taken as an attributive description by way of ascription (*al-wasf al-iddda'i*), in the manner of an eloquent simile (*al-tashbih al-baligh*), as

[Page 67]

al-Mutanabbi made the people who left their guest, although they were able to keep him, as travellers departing from their guest, in his saying:

*When you depart from a people who were able not to part from them, the departing ones are they.*

It may also be that *al-maftun* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) on the pattern of the *maf'ul*, like *al-ma'qul* meaning reason, *al-majlud* meaning flogging, and *al-maysur* meaning ease, with *al-ma'sur* as its opposite; and in the proverb: "Take from what is easy of him and leave what is difficult of him." On this view, the *ba'* is for accompaniment (*al-mulabasah*), in the position of a predicate fronted before *al-maftun*, which is the subject (*mubtada'*).

The verb ﴿tubsiru yubsiruna﴾ is taken to imply the sense of: you will be certain and they will be certain, by way of metonymy (*kinayah*) of the act of seeing for verification, because the strongest of the senses is sight. The bringing of the *ba'* is to indicate this implication. The meaning: you will know with certainty, and they will know with certainty, which of you is the afflicted one. So the *ba'* stays with its original transitive function, attached to ﴿tubsiru yubsiruna﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 7:

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾

This is a justification (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿So you will see and they will see﴾ [al-Qalam: 5] ﴿which of you is the afflicted (al-maftun)﴾ [al-Qalam: 6], in view of what it contains by way of allusion (ta'ridh) that the afflicted party is the party that said to him (﴿Indeed, you are a madman﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]), and that its opposite, by its opposite, is the one who has sound reason. That is, the one who informed you, through what He alluded to in His words ﴿So you will see and they will see﴾ [al-Qalam: 5], that they are the madmen, is the most knowing of the two groups. He is the One who told you that the truth will become clear to their eyes. Thus it is established that the afflicted party is the group who labelled the Prophet ﷺ as a madman, which is refuted by His words, exalted is He, ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2], since they are, without doubt, the ones who have strayed from the way of the Lord of the Prophet ﷺ. Gradually, from the beginning of the surah up to this point, there is an arrangement of equality syllogisms (aqyisat musawat), some of which are contained within others, which require the equivalence of the reality of one who has strayed from the paths of the Lord of the Prophet ﷺ with the reality of the afflicted, and the equivalence of the reality of the afflicted with the reality of the madman. Thus it follows that the group of polytheists are the ones characterised by madness, according to the principle of the equality syllogism: that which is equal to an equal is equal to that same thing.

Page 68

This transition contains both a promise and a warning, by attributing the way (al-sabil) to God and by setting those who have strayed from it against those who are guided.

The generality of "those who have strayed from His way" and the generality of "those who are guided" makes this clause, while also serving as a proof, likewise a concluding appendage (tadhyil).

Beyond all of this, it is a preface (tamhid) and preparation (tawti'a) for His words ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 8].

[p. 68]

﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ ﴿They wish you would soften, so they would soften﴾. This is a consequence of the sentence ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾ [al-Qalam: 7] to its end, in view of what it contains: that the Prophet is upon guidance, and that the other side is in the straying from the path. This requires firmness with them and that he not yield to them in anything, since their harm to him leads to fighting the truth and guidance, and to obstinacy in the misguidance they are upon, away from the way of God. They therefore do not deserve gentleness from him, but deserve harshness.

Al-Kalbi, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Hasan related, in closely similar wordings revolving around the same meaning, that the polytheists wished that the Prophet (ﷺ) would refrain from openly denouncing them as misguided and belittling them, so that they would refrain from harming him, and that each side would accommodate the other. God therefore forbade him from responding to what they wished.

The meaning of "wadd" (wished) is: they loved.

It is not intended that they wished this in their own souls, such that God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of it, since that does not fit with His saying ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾.

The books of the biography (sirah) report that the polytheists approached the Prophet (ﷺ) with a proposal of this kind, and made intermediaries in this matter his uncle Abu Talib and Utba ibn Rabi'a.

Thus it is coherent that His saying ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ is a prohibition against responding to them with anything they proposed to him, at the time when he rebuked them at the beginning of this surah, especially given the wonderful effect of the allusion, mingled with a threat of bad outcome, in His saying ﴿So you will see and they will see﴾ [al-Qalam: 5] ﴿which of you is the afflicted﴾ [al-Qalam: 6], up to His saying "the guided". Perhaps they spoke among themselves, or instructed someone to inform the Messenger (ﷺ), or told him directly that if their saying about him ﴿Indeed, he is a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] displeased him, then [p. 69] it displeased them that he belittled them with descriptions of blame and belittled their idols and their forefathers from the side of disbelief. If he refrained from that, they would refrain from harming him, and the situation would be a reconciliation between them, each party leaving the other and what it worships.

Obedience (ta'a) is: accepting what is sought to be done. The verb "tuti'" (obey) occurring in the scope of a prohibition requires the prohibition of the category of obedience to them, so it covers every response to a request from them. Obedience here therefore means reconciliation and softness, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [al-Furqan: 52], meaning: do not be soft toward them.

The description of them as "deniers" was chosen over other ways of identifying them, because it is equivalent to a relative clause in indicating the basis for the ruling, which is the prohibition of obeying them: the prohibition of obeying them is because they denied his message.

From here it becomes clear that the clause ﴿They wish you would soften, so they would soften﴾ explains the object of the forbidden obedience, and for this reason it is separated and not conjoined.

The verb "tudhinu" (you soften) is derived from "idhan", which is softening and accommodating. The literal sense of this verb is to make something have oil (duhn), either to soften it or to color it. From these two meanings the various senses of idhan branched out, as al-Raghib indicated. That is: they wished from you that you would soften toward them, so that they would soften toward you; that is, if you were to meet them with good treatment, they would meet you with the like.

The "fa" in "fa-yudhinun" (so they soften) is for conjunction and for causation, following the clause "law tudhinu" (if you were to soften), as an answer to the sense of wishing indicated by the verb "wadda" (they wished). Rather, it is intended to explain the cause of their wish. Therefore the verb after the "fa" was not put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" (that), because the "fa" of causation is sufficient to convey this. The sentence is then taken as having an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "fa-hum yudhinun" (so they soften). He adopted this construction so that the implied noun would precede the verbal predicate, thereby conveying the meaning of exclusivity: that is, softening comes from them, not from you; that is, abandon softening toward them and do not take on its character yourself. This is a manner of usage when what is intended by the sequence is that it is not the conditioning of an answer, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever believes in his Lord, then he does not fear deficiency or burden﴾ [al-Jinn: 13], meaning: so he does not fear deficiency or burden.

The particle "law" (if/that) may be conditional, with "tudhinu" as the condition and its answer omitted; the estimate being: "law tudhinu la-hasala lahum ma yawaddunna" (if you were to soften, there would come to them what they wish). It may also be a verbal-nominal particle (masdariyyah) according to the view of a group of grammarians of Arabic, that "law" comes as a particle like "an" (that). This was said by al-Farra', al-Farisi, al-Tibrizi and Ibn Malik. The estimate would then be: "wadda idhanaka" (they wished your softening).

The object of "wadda" is omitted, indicated by "law tudhinu", or it is the verbal noun itself, on the basis that "law" functions as a verbal-nominal particle. This was discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿One of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96] in Surat al-Baqarah. The placement of the "fa" may also indicate that their wish for him to soften is a reason: they wish that from you because they themselves are softeners, and whoever has an evil intention wishes that people be like him.

﴿And do not obey every habitual swearer﴾. The verb of prohibition concerning obedience is repeated for those who have these attributes, to give emphasis to this admonition. He did not suffice with including the people of these attributes within the general scope of the deniers, nor with singling them out by mere conjunction of the particular with the general, by saying "and not every swearer." Rather, in their case a different prohibitive form, similar to the first, was used.

It serves to direct the particular threat, which is implied in His saying ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾ [al-Qalam: 16], at the people of these particular attributes, in addition to the threat against the deniers.

Close to this is the verse of al-Harith ibn Hammam al-Shaybani:

"O son of Zayyaba, if you meet me, do not meet me among the scattered camels,
but meet me, where a swift, bare-backed horse runs with me, its leader at the pool like a rider."

He did not suffice with a conjunction by *bal* ("rather") or *lakin* ("but") by saying: "Rather, you meet me, where a swift horse runs with me," or "But you meet me, where a swift horse runs with me." Instead he departed from that and repeated the verb *talqani* ("you meet me").

The word *kull* (كُلَّ, "every") is laid down to express totality and comprehensiveness over the individual members of the noun to which it is attached. Here it expresses a general prohibition against obeying each individual of the people of these attributes, to whom *kull* is attached directly and through the descriptive qualities.

The word *kull* (كُلَّ) has come as the object of the verb upon which the particle of prohibition enters. It should not be understood from this that the prohibition is directed at obeying a person in whom all these attributes are combined, such that if he obeyed some of the people of these attributes he would not be violating the prohibition. This does not occur to the mind, nor does it accord with the usages of the language. Rather, the intended meaning is a prohibition against obeying each person characterised by one of these traits, let alone one in whom several of them are combined.

In this there is a refutation of what Shaykh Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) established in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* concerning the distinction between *kull* falling within the scope of negation (or prohibition), which yields the affirmation of the act or attribute for some of what *kull* is attached to, if *kull* is the subject; or yields the connection of the act or attribute to some of what *kull* is attached to, if *kull* is the object of the negated or prohibited verb; and between *kull* falling outside the scope of negation. He also made the raising of the word *kulluhu* in the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"Umm al-Khiyar has begun to claim against me a sin, all of which I did not commit,"

to be necessarily so; for if he had put it in the accusative, it would express his disclaimer of having committed the whole of what she alleged against him of sins, and so it would be credible that he committed some of those sins, which he did not intend, as the scholar al-Taftazani clearly stated in *al-Mutawwal* refuting this. He cited in support of the refutation His saying ﴿God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276] and His saying ﴿And do not obey every habitual swearer, despicable﴾.

The prohibition concerning obedience has been applied to these blameworthy attributes, because their possessors are not fit to be obeyed; there is no trust in them, and they only command evil.

A group of exegetes (mufassirun) said that the intended referent of "the habitual swearer, despicable" is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Some said it is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. Others said it is al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth. Among the exegetes is one who said the intended referent is Abu Jahl. What they meant is that the intended purpose is an allusion to one of these men; otherwise the word *kull* (كَلَّ), which expresses generality, does not permit that the prohibition be directed at one specific individual. As for these men, perhaps the four of them shared most of these attributes, so they are among those intended by the prohibition against obeying, and whoever is of their kind among their likes.

The intended meaning is not one who combines all these qualities, but rather one who possesses even one of them. The gravest of these qualities is denying the Qur'an, which is concluded by His saying ﴿when Our signs are recited to him, he says: "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [al-Qalam: 15]. But the one who said of the Qur'an that "it is tales of the ancients" was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He is the one who fabricated this calumny in a well-known account. When the others took up this calumny from him and were impressed by it, they began to repeat it, so all of them became among those who say it. For this reason God attributed this statement to them in the verse ﴿And they said: "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [al-Furqan: 5].

Ten of their blameworthy qualities are mentioned. The first is *hallaf* (حَلّاف, "habitual swearer"). The *hallaf* is one who frequently swears oaths upon his promises and his reports. I think that what is intended by it is a metonym for indifference to lying and to false oaths. The intensive form was used as a metonym for deliberately breaking oaths; otherwise his censure would not be of this degree. Among the exegetes is one who made *mahin* (مَهِين, "despicable") a restrictive qualifier of *hallaf*, on the basis that the prohibition on obeying the possessor of the attribute applies to both together.

* * *

[Page 72]

*Mahin* (مَهِين, "despicable") is a second quality, and it is not a qualifier of *hallaf*.

*Mahin*, with a fatha on the *mim*, is on the pattern *fa'il* from *mahuna* (مَهُنَ), meaning "to be lowly and humiliated." It is thus an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha). Its verb is *mahuna* with a damma on the *ha*; its *mim* is original and its *ya* is additional. It is *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active participle), i.e., "do not obey the wicked, the lowly." *Mahin* here may also mean "weak in judgement and discernment." All of these derive from *mahana* (humiliation).

*Mahin* is an adjective (na't) of *hallaf*. The same applies to the rest of the qualities up to *zanim* (زَنِيم, "ignoble"), so it is an independent adjective. Some made it a qualifier of *hallaf* and interpreted *mahin* as "the liar," i.e., in his swearing.

**[Verse 11]** ﴿*hammāzin*﴾ *al-Hammāz* is one who frequently engages in *hamz*. The root meaning of *hamz* is stabbing with a stick or a hand. The word was extended metaphorically (*istiʿāra*, the use of a word in a figurative sense) to harm inflicted through speech by backbiting, and this usage became so common that it came to function like a literal meaning. In the Revelation, it is said: ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer﴾ [al-Humazah: 1].

The intensive form (*ṣīghat al-mubālaghah*, the pattern expressing emphasis or intensity) refers to the strength of the attribute. If the harm is severe, its doer is *hammāz*. If the harm is repeated, its doer is also *hammāz*.

* * *

﴿*mashshāʾin bi-namīmin*﴾ *al-Mashshāʾ bi-l-namīm* is one who goes about among people carrying tale-bearing. He is described as *mashshāʾ* for the sake of intensity. What is said about this intensive form is the same as what was said about (*hammāz*), and this is the fourth of the blameworthy traits.

Page 73

The word *mashy* (walking) is a metaphor that depicts his condition as one who undergoes hardship for the sake of tale-bearing, similar to the mention of striving in His saying, ﴿and they strive throughout the land to cause corruption﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. The reason is that names of perceptible things have a stronger impact on the hearer's imagination than names of abstract concepts. Thus the mention of walking in tale-bearing portrays the state of the tale-bearer. Do you not see that your saying "his head was cut off" strikes the soul more forcefully than your saying "he was killed"? This is supported by the fact that a similar expression occurs in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «As for the other, he used to walk about spreading tale-bearing».

*Al-namīm* is a noun synonymous with *al-namīmah* (tale-bearing). It has also been said that *al-namīm* is the plural of *namīmah*, meaning a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*, a noun with plural sense but not following regular plural patterns) for *namīmah*, when the singular is intended and it has become a noun in its own right.

﴿Mannā'in lil-khayr﴾ (withholding of good): this is the fifth reproach.

Mannā' means one who is extremely withholding. Al-khayr here means wealth, that is, stingy with wealth. Khayr is among the names of wealth. God the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8], and He says: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. The same pattern has been observed in these four attributes, namely "hallaf, hammaz, mashsha', mannā'," and this is a type of the embellishment of balance (muhassin al-muwazanah).

What is meant by withholding good is withholding it from those among their kin and relatives who embraced Islam. One of them would say to a family member or client who had become Muslim: "Whoever among you enters the religion of Muhammad, I will never benefit him with anything, ever." This was a habit by which they became known thereafter. God the Exalted said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse."﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. Also, among withholding good is that the people of the Jahiliyyah would give gifts for pride and reputation, so they would not give to the weak; rather, they would give in gatherings and tribal assemblies. God the Exalted said: ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr: 18]. It is said that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah would spend, on every pilgrimage, twenty thousand (dirhams), feeding the people of Mina, yet he would not give the poor man a single dirham.

* * *

﴿Mu'tadin athim﴾ (aggressor, sinful): these are the sixth and seventh reproaches. He joined them together because of the relation of specific and general.
I'tida' is an intensification of transgression, so the iftial form in it indicates intensity.

Page 74

Athim means one who commits much sin, and it is fa'il, one of the intensive patterns. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43], ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44]. What is meant by ithm here is that which is considered a wrong and corruption in the eyes of people of intellect and honor, and in the known religions.
Abu Hayyan said: These attributes came as intensive attributes, and the nun was coordinated (nuwasiba) in them: thus he came with "hallaf," followed by "mahin," because the nun in them is in harmony with the mim, that is, the mim of "athim." Then came ﴿hammaz mashsha'﴾ [al-Qalam: 11] with the two intensive attributes. Then came ﴿mannā'in lil-khayr mu'tadin athim﴾ as intensive attributes, end quote. He means that the iftial in mu'tadin is for intensification.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 13–14:

﴿Cruel, moreover, and of doubtful birth.﴾ Eighth and ninth.

Al-'Utull (with two dammas and a doubled lam) is a noun, not a descriptive adjective, but it carries the sense of a descriptive term, because it is derived from al-'atl (with a fatha and then a sukun), which means to push forcefully. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Dukhan: 47]. The form (ʿātil) is not attested. Among the evidence that it belongs to the category of nouns rather than adjectives is that it is compounded of two descriptive terms in different states, or of a compound of descriptive terms in two different states.

Al-'Utull has been interpreted as "one of harsh build and wide belly," as "one who eats and drinks greedily," as "one who is oppressive and tyrannical," and as "one who is fleshy and arrogant." Al-Mawardi related this interpretation from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Ibn Mas'ud, from Shaddad ibn Aws, and from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, with some of them adding to others, from the Prophet (ﷺ), through a chain that is not strong. According to this interpretation, it is a continuation of the description ﴿withholding from the good﴾ [al-Qalam: 12], meaning that he prevents the beggar, repels him, and treats him harshly, similar to the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿That is the one who repulses the orphan﴾ [al-Ma'un: 2].

The meaning of ﴿after that﴾ is: in addition to what has been enumerated of his descriptions, he is ill-favoured in build and ill in dealing. Here the "after" is a sequence in ascending the degrees of the stated description, so its function is that of the sequential delay of rank, as in the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30], according to one of the two interpretations of it.

According to the interpretation of al-'Utull as one of harsh build and wide belly, the reason for mentioning it is that the ugliness of his person completes his defects, because a visible flaw is more conducive to aversion and penetrates more deeply into revulsion from its bearer.

The position of (after that) is that of a parenthetical clause, and the adverbial phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: he is, after that.

It is permissible for (after that) to be connected to the word (zanim) as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of (zanim).

Al-Zanim is the attached one, namely the one who is a claimed outsider among his people, not of their pure lineage, either because of a blemish in his descent, or because he is an ally of a people or a client (mawla). It is derived from al-zanama (with a fatha and then a sukun), which is a piece of a camel's ear that is not torn off but remains hanging from the ear as a sign of the camel's nobility. The two zanamatan are two pieces at the necks of goats.

It has been said that the zanim intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, because his father claimed him eighteen years after his birth. It has also been said that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq is intended, because he was from Thaqif, allied himself with Quraysh, and settled among them. Whatever is intended by it, the intended one is particular, so his inclusion in the coordinated item attached to what (kull) is annexed to is only on the assumption of the existence of similar particular cases, and this is a kind of symbolism, as one says: "What is the matter with people who do such-and-such," meaning one specific person. Al-Khatim al-Tamimi, a pre-Islamic poet, or Hassan ibn Thabit, said:

A zanim whom men claimed as an addition, as the forearms are added to the stretched hide.

The term zanim is also applied to one who has a stain in his lineage from the side of the mothers. From this is the saying of Hassan in satirizing Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, before Abu Sufyan's conversion to Islam, whose mother was a client (mawla), unlike the rest of the Banu Hashim, since their mothers were of the pure lineage of their people:

And you are a zanim, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider.

Indeed the summit of glory is from the family of Hashim; the sons of the daughter of Makhzum, and your father is the slave ('Abd).

He means his grandfather, the maternal father, who was Muwhib, the freed slave of 'Abd Manaf. The mother of Abu Sufyan was Sumayya, daughter of this Muwhib.

The discussion of this general usage and of what is intended by it is similar to the discussion of the general usage that preceded it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 15:

﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "These are the fables of the ancients."﴾

Page 76
The phrase ﴿because he has wealth and sons﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] is connected to the verb (qala, "he said"), with an elided lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) assumed before (an, "because"). This is an ellipsis that is regularly employed. Attached to that verb are an adverbial phrase, which is ﴿when it is recited﴾, and a prepositional phrase, which is ﴿because he has wealth﴾ [al-Qalam: 14]. There is nothing strange in this, and (idha, "when") is not conditional here. Therefore do not be alarmed by the claim that (ma, "what") following a conditional particle cannot govern what precedes it. Moreover, even if it were made conditional, that would not be impossible, since they allow more latitude with prepositional phrases than with other constructions, and this one is governed by the elided lam.

The meaning is: every person who has wealth and sons among the great unbelievers, as in His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the people of plenty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. It has been said that what is intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, since he is the one who fabricated the claim that the Qur'an consists of "fables of the ancients." You already know this from the explanation of His saying, ﴿And do not obey every swearing, contemptible one﴾ [al-Qalam: 10]. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira had abundant wealth and many sons, and he is the one referred to in His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], ﴿and to whom I gave extensive wealth﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 12], ﴿and sons present﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 13], up to His saying, ﴿This is nothing but the speech of a human being﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25]. The more apt view is that this description is not restricted to him, and that it is an allusion to him.

Al-asatir (fables) is the plural of ustura, which means a story. Ustura is a word arabicized from the Roman (Greek) language, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Those who disbelieve say: this is nothing but fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am: 25] in al-An'am, and His saying, ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the ancients"﴾ [al-Nahl: 24] in Surat al-Nahl.

The descriptions warning against obeying their bearers were concluded with the attribute of denial, so as to return to the attribute of denial from which the discourse shifted, from His saying, ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 8].

The majority read ﴿an kana dha mal﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] with a single hamza, taking it as a declarative statement. Hamza and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read it with two lightened hamzas, making it an interrogative of denial. Ibn 'Amir read it with a hamza and a madda, making the second hamza an alif for lightening.

[p. 77]

**"We will brand him upon the snout"** (﴿سَنَسِمُهُ عَلى الخُرْطُومِ﴾) is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an unstated question). It answers a question the listener would naturally ask after the description of these blameworthy qualities: what is the recompense from God for the people who have these attributes, given the vile deeds they committed and their audacity toward their Lord?

The singular pronoun in His words *sanasimuhu* ("We will brand him") refers to every *haffar* (habitual oath-swearer) taken in terms of the word's form, even though its meaning is plural. So the singular form of its pronoun is like the singular form of the attributes that follow *kull* ("every"), which came in the singular.

The meaning is: We will brand all of these on the snouts. You have already learned that this is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to a specific person, by the attribute of His words, **"tales of the ancients"** (﴿أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ [al-Qalam: 15]), and by the fact that he has wealth and sons.

*Al-khurtum* is meant here as the nose. The apparent sense is that the literal meaning of *al-khurtum* is the elongated nose, like the nose of an elephant, a pig, and the like, any elongated nose. The lexicographers mixed up its meanings to such a degree that its literal meaning cannot be distinguished from its figurative meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) mentioned its figurative meanings in *al-Asas*, but did not mention its literal meaning. His statement in *al-Kashshaf* is ambiguous, except that his words there, "In the word *al-khurtum* there is contempt and humiliation," imply that applying it to the human nose is a metonymy of the general type (*majaz mursal*). Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 542 AH) asserted decisively that the literal meaning of *al-khurtum* is the muzzle (*mikhtam*) of a predator, i.e., its snout, like that of a lion. Therefore applying *al-khurtum* to the human nose here is a metaphor (*isti'arah*), like applying *al-mishfar* (the lip of a camel, which is the camel's lip) to the human lip, in the words of al-Farazdaq:

*Had you been a Dabbi, you would have known my kinship,*
*But you are a Zanji with thick lips.*

And like applying *al-jahfalah* (the lip of horses, mules and donkeys) to the human lip, in the words of al-Nabigha, satirizing Labid ibn Rabi'a:

*Is there anyone who will convey from me to Labid,*
*Abu al-Warda, the big lip of the she-ass?*

*Al-wasm* for camels and the like means placing a brand on them, indicating that they are the property of a particular tribe or specific owner.

So the meaning is: We will treat him in a manner by which it will be known that he is Our slave, and that his wealth and his children will not avail him anything from Us.

Thus *al-wasm* is an image (*tamthil*), followed by a metonymy (*kinayah*) for having power over him and displaying his helplessness.

The original form of *(nasimuhu)* is *nusimuhu*, like *ya'idu* and *yasilu*.

Mentioning the *khurtum* in it combines disfigurement and humiliation. Branding implies gaining control, and its being on the face is a humiliation and debasement, and its being on the nose is even more debasing. Referring to the nose as *al-khurtum* is disfigurement. Striking or branding the nose and the like is a metonymy for the strength of control and complete domination, and for the helplessness of the owner of the nose to resist, because the nose is the most prominent feature of the face and the passage of breath. For this reason, mention of the nose predominates in expressing display of pride in the phrase "he raised his nose" (*shamakha bi-anfihi*), and he has "raised noses" (*shumm al-'aranin*). Conversely, the expression of the manifestation of abasement and submission is "breaking the nose," "cutting off the nose," and "its falling into the dust," as in the phrases "his nose was rubbed in the dirt" (*raghima anfuhu*) and "in spite of his nose" (*'ala raghmi anfihi*). Jarir said:

*When I placed my brand on al-Farazdaq,*
*And on al-Bu'ayth I cut off the nose of al-Akhtal.*

Most of the exegetes hold that the one intended by this threat is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said in his tafsir: His words *"We will brand him upon the snout"* refer to what God afflicted him with in himself, his wealth, and his family of evil, humiliation and disgrace. He means: what befell them on the day of Badr and what came after it until the conquest of Makkah.

From Ibn 'Abbas, regarding *"We will brand him upon the snout,"* the meaning is: "We will strike his nose with the sword." He said: The one about whom it was revealed had his nose struck with the sword on the day of Badr, and he remained with a struck nose until he died. Ibn 'Abbas did not specify who he was.

When they struck with swords, they aimed at faces and heads. The Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of Badr to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he was informed of the statement of Abu Hudhayfah, "If I meet al-'Abbas, I will strike him with the sword": "O Abu Hafs, is the face of the uncle of the Messenger of God to be struck with the sword?"

It has also been said that this is a threat to disfigure his nose on the Day of Resurrection, like His words, **"On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black"** (﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]). His disfigurement on that day was made to be in his nose, because he only went to extremes in enmity toward the Messenger and in attacking the religion out of pride and arrogance, and the nose was the place where arrogance shows. For this reason pride was called *anafah* (haughtiness), derived from the name of the nose. So his disfigurement was placed where the traces of his pride appear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 17–25 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the people of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning,﴾ ﴿and did not make an exception.﴾ ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep.﴾ ﴿So it became like the black, harvested night.﴾ ﴿Then they called out to one another in the morning,﴾ ﴿"Go out early to your field, if you are going to harvest."﴾ ﴿So they set out, whispering to one another,﴾ ﴿"Let no poor person enter it today against you."﴾ ﴿And they went early, with a determination, as those capable.﴾

The pronoun of the absent in His saying "bala'nahum" (We tried them) returns to the deniers mentioned in His saying ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 8]. The sentence is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), prompted by the connection with His saying ﴿because he has wealth and sons﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 15]. For arrogance (izdiha') and conceit (ghurur) arising from abundance of provision, which lead to slighting the call to truth and neglecting to consider its reality and its proofs, have from ancient times brought their possessors into the ingratitude of blessings and the neglect of thanks, and that drew upon them the worst of outcomes. So God struck for the polytheists an example from the condition of the people of this garden, perhaps they would awaken from their heedlessness and conceit. He likewise struck a similar example in Surat al-Kahf, and struck an example with Qarun in Surat al-Qasas.

Al-balwa (the trial) in its reality means testing, and here it is a figure for the condition of one being tested by letting out the rope to him with blessing, so that he may be thankful or ungrateful. So the trial mentioned here is a trial by good: God granted the people of Makkah the blessing of security and the blessing of provision, made provision come to them from every direction, and facilitated for them the paths of trade across the regions through the blessing of the "Ilaf" (the journeys of winter and summer). Then, when He completed for them the blessing by sending a messenger from among them, to complete for them the good of their affairs and guide them to what holds lasting bliss, he called them and reminded them of God's blessings, they turned away and transgressed, and did not turn to consider the earlier blessings nor the complete blessing which completed all their blessings.

The aspect of resemblance between their condition and the condition of the people of the garden mentioned here is turning away from seeking God's good pleasure and from thanking His blessing.

This figure is an allusive threat that there will befall them what befell the people of the garden: misery after bliss, and dearth after plenty. Although the cause differs in kind, its genus is one. This occurred after some years, when God seized them with seven years after the Prophet's ﷺ migration to Madinah.

This story by which the example is struck is well known among them: there was in a land called Darawan (with a dotted dad, a ra, a waw, all with fatha, an alif and a nun), in the lands of Yemen near Sana'a. It is said: Darawan is the name of this garden. It was a great garden planted by a man of righteousness and faith from the People of the Book, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. He did not specify which of the People of the Book he was: was he from the Jews or the Christians? It is said he was a Jew, meaning because the people of Yemen had adopted Judaism in the time of Bilqis, as it is said, or after her by the migration of some of Sulayman's soldiers, and the giving of the zakat on fruits was part of the Torah's law, as in the sixteenth chapter [sic: twenty-sixth] of the Book of Leviticus.

Some exegetes said: the people of this garden were shortly after 'Isa, that is, before Christianity spread in Yemen, for it did not enter Yemen except after the Abyssinians entered Yemen in the story of al-Qulleis, and that was at the time of the Year of the Elephant. And from 'Ikrimah: they were from Abyssinia. Their father had a garden, and he set aside a portion of its fruit for the needy, and he would bring the needy with him to take from its fruits. Orphans, widows and the needy lived from it. He had three sons. When the owner of the garden died and it passed to his children, they became people of wealth, and they were stingy, or some of them were stingy and some less so. So they agreed together to deprive the orphans, the needy and the widows, and said: "We will surely go to the garden in the darkness of the night before the morning breaks, like the time when people go out to their gardens to harvest, so we will harvest it before the needy come." They planned this and swore oaths upon it, and perhaps they swore in order to bind themselves to carrying out what they had agreed upon. This implies that some of them were hesitant to agree with them on what they had resolved, and that they bound him with the oath. This accords with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The best of them said, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify God?'"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28]. It is said: he would say to them, "Fear God, and turn away from the wickedness of your intention in withholding from the needy," and he reminded them of God's retribution against the wrongdoers. So they overpowered him and proceeded to what they had resolved upon. Perhaps they swore to do it and swore that he would do it with them, so he swore with them or agreed to what they had sworn upon. For this reason the oath is attributed to all the people of the garden.

So when they came to their garden, they found it blackened, having been struck by what resembles burning. When they saw it in that state, they knew that this had befallen them alone, because of their resolve to cut off what the weak of their people benefited from, and they turned in repentance to God, hoping that He would give them something better than it.

It is said: this garden was of grapes.

Al-sarm: cutting the fruit and harvesting it.

﴿Muslihin﴾ means entering into the morning, that is, at the beginning of dawn.

The meaning of ﴿they do not make an exception﴾ is that they make no exception from the fruit for the needy, that is, they swore they would surely harvest all the fruit and leave nothing of it. This generality is derived from what is in sarm of the meaning of storing and benefiting from the fruit, for otherwise sarm does not preclude giving some of the harvest to whomever they wish. This was left general, relying on what is known to the listeners of the details of this story, according to the Qur'an's custom of brevity in narrating stories, by confining itself to the point of lesson in them.

It is also said its meaning is: they do not make an exception by saying "if God wills," as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And do not say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] ﴿unless God wills﴾ [al-Kahf: 24]. The reason it is called an exception (istithna') is that the original form of the expression contains the particle of exception, which is "illa" (except). When someone limits himself to "in sha' Allah" without the particle of exception, that statement is called an exception, since it is by way of the presumption: "except that God wills." Moreover, since the condition returns to the meaning of exception, it is called an exception by considering the meaning and the root from which "istithna'" is derived.

On this interpretation, His saying "and they do not make an exception" is of the kind of idmaj (insertion), that is, due to the extent of their conceit in their own strength, when they resolved upon doing something they did not expect any obstacle to it. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the expression with the present verb is to bring to mind their strange condition of stinginess toward the poor and the orphans.

According to all the reports, it is known that the people of this garden were not disbelievers, so the aspect of resemblance between them and the polytheists to whom this example is struck is the ingratitude of blessing and the delusion of strength.

His saying ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord﴾: al-tawaf is walking around something from all its sides; it is said "tafa bil-Ka'bah" (he circumambulated the Ka'bah). It is intended here as a figure for the condition of striking a whole thing with the condition of one who circles a place, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿When a visitation from Satan touches them﴾ [al-A'raf: 201], and so on.

The verb (tafa) is transitive with the particle (ʿalā) by virtue of its being construed with the meaning of: "to overpower" or "to descend upon."

He did not specify the kind of the visitor, since it is evident that it is of the kind of what strikes gardens with destruction, and no purpose depends on specifying its type, because the lesson lies in what results from it. So ascribing the verb (tafa) to a visitor is like ascribing the verb in the passive voice, as if it were said: "it was circled over them while they were
asleep."

It is related from al-Farra' that the visitor is only at night, meaning that from this the dream-image which one sees in his sleep is called "tayf." It is said it is derived from "ta'ifah," which is a portion of the night. There is room for scrutiny in this.

So His saying ﴿while they were asleep﴾ is a restriction of the time of the visitor according to the first interpretation, and it is an emphasis of the meaning of "visitor" according to al-Farra's interpretation, and its benefit is depicting the condition.

The tanwin of "ta'if" is for magnification, that is, a great matter, and He has explained it by His saying ﴿So it became like the black, harvested night﴾. So it is an evil visitation. It is said: a neck of fire reached it and it was burned.

And ﴿from your Lord﴾ means coming from the side of your Lord, so "min" here is for origin, meaning that it was a punishment sent down upon them as a retribution for their failure to give thanks for the blessing.

The punishment was hastened for them before they were engaged in withholding charity, because their resolve to withhold and their mutual agreement upon it effectively established that they were withholding their charity, so they were withholding. From the verse a warning is derived for those who do not console others with their wealth.

Since the punishment of the people of this garden was worldly, there is nothing in the verse indicating that the people of the garden withheld obligatory charity.

As for al-sarim: it is said it is the night, and sarim is among the names of the night and among the names of the day, because each of them is cut off from the other, just as each of the night and the day is called "malwan," so it is said "al-malawan." On this basis, the combination of "asbahat" (it became) and "al-sarim" contains the figure of antithesis (tibaq).

It is said: al-sarim is the black ash, in the dialect of Judhaymah or Khuzaymah.

It is said: al-sarim is the name of a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing.

The choice of the word al-sarim here is due to the abundance of its meanings and the suitability of all those meanings to be intended in the verse.

Between "yasrimunnaha" and "al-sarim" there is paronomasia (jinas).

The fa' of ﴿Then they called out﴾ is for consequence upon ﴿they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning﴾, that is, when they woke in the morning they called to one another to carry out what they had plotted.

Al-tanadi: that some of them call out to others, and it implies encouragement to go out to their garden early.

Al-ghuduw: going out and leaving a place at the early part of the day, that is, its beginning.

Their saying ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾ is not a conditional clause, but it is used for urging on the slow. It is as if, due to the slowness of some of them in going out, they had turned from harvesting that day. From it is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar to al-Hajjaj at the decline of the sun on 'Arafah, urging him to hasten to the standing place: "Go early, if you want the Sunnah." And similar to this is abundant in speech.

The "ʿalā" in His saying ﴿upon your field﴾ is used to express the attainability of reaching it, as if it were said: "Go out, and be upon your field," that is, settled upon it.

It is also possible that the verb "ghuduw" is construed with the meaning of "approach," as one says: "He is brought his bowl in the morning and in the evening." Al-Tibi said: a similar thing was said regarding al-Muttalib: his whip (with which he strikes) is cast upon the foolish, and his bowl upon the forbearing.

Al-harth: cleaving the earth with an iron tool or the like, so that seed or trees may be placed in it, and so that grass may be removed from it.

Al-harth is also applied to the garden, since they tend it by cultivating it to improve its trees, and this is what is meant here, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and cultivated land, forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 138] in Surat al-An'am, and it has preceded in His saying ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-takhafut: a reciprocal form from "khafata," meaning to speak secretly.

﴿Let no poor person enter it today against you﴾ is an explanation of the act of "yatakhafatun" (whispering), and "an" is explanatory, because the whispering carries the sense of speech without its letters.

The emphasis of the prohibitive verb with the emphatic nun is to add further confirmation to what they had agreed upon.

The prohibitive verb is ascribed to "miskin" (poor person) regarding the prohibition of entering, and what is meant is that some of them forbid others from letting a poor person enter their garden, that is, no one leaves a poor person to enter it. This is of the kind of kinayah (metonymy), which is common in the use of the prohibition, as in their saying: "I shall not find you doing such and such."

His saying ﴿and they went early, with a determination, as those capable﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause with the implied "qad," that is, they set out while being early-goers, capable of a determination.

The verb "ghadaw" is mentioned in the circumstantial clause for the purpose of marvelling at that ill-omened early departure, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*He spent the night, and a night was for him like the night of one with the sore, blear eye.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 17–25 (part 2 of 2):

After his saying:
*"Long has your night stretched out at al-Athmud,
and the one free of care has spent the night while you did not sleep."*

He addresses his own soul in a manner that contains an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) or two shifts.

Al-ḥard (حَرْد) is used to mean prevention, to mean strong intent, that is, haste, and to mean anger.

In the choice of the word (ḥardin) in the verse there is one of the subtleties of i'jaz (the inimitability of the Qur'an), concerning the eloquence of the word and its refinement in meaning, and concerning how the prepositional phrase relates to it in a way that suits each of its meanings. That is, the phrase (ʿalā ḥardin) may be linked to (qādirīna), or to the verb (ghadawā).

If it is linked to (qādirīna), then placing the complement first gives a restriction: *able to prevent*, that is, able to prevent good, or to prevent the fruit of their garden, while unable to benefit.

Expressing it as *qādirīna ʿalā ḥardin* rather than saying *wa-ghadaw ḥādirīna* is a taḥakkum (mockery). The usage of the verb of ability (qudra) is customarily mentioned with actions that are difficult for people to perform. God the Exalted says: ﴿They have no power over anything they have earned﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], and He says: ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyama: 4]. So His saying ﴿upon ḥardin, able﴾, according to this possibility, is of the type of their saying: "So-and-so owns nothing but deprivation," or "is able to achieve nothing but failure."

If ḥard is taken to mean haste and intent, then (ʿalā ḥardin) is linked to (ghadawā), explaining the kind of morning-going: that is, they went out with a morning-going of haste and eagerness. In this case (ʿalā) carries the meaning of the bāʾ of accompaniment (bā' al-musāḥaba), and the sense is: going out early with speed and vigor. And (qādirīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in (ghadawā), a ḥāl muqaddara (a clause anticipated in meaning), that is, presuming that they were able to achieve what they wanted.

In the speech there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) that they failed, indicated by His saying after it: ﴿When they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have surely gone astray"﴾ [al-Qalam: 26], and His saying before it: ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep﴾.

[Page 85]

If ḥard is meant as anger and rage, it is said ḥaradun with a vowel on the rāʾ and ḥardun with the rāʾ unvowelled. The prepositional phrase is then linked to (qādirīna), and placing it first gives restriction: that is, they went out having no ability except for rage and anger against the poor, because they would break into their garden every day. So they schemed against them by going early to harvest it. That is, they had no power except for anger and rage, and they were unable to do what they had intended, which was to gather the fruit of the garden.

From al-Suddi: that *ḥardin* is the name of their village, that is, their garden. I think this is a patched-together interpretation, and it seems its author derived it from the two verbs (ughdū) and (ghadawā).

Their saying ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾ is not a conditional clause, but it is used for urging on the slow. It is as if, due to the slowness of some of them in going out, they had turned from harvesting that day. From it is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar to al-Hajjaj at the decline of the sun on 'Arafah, urging him to hasten to the standing place: "Go early, if you want the Sunnah." And similar to this is abundant in speech.

The "ʿalā" in His saying ﴿upon your field﴾ is used to express the attainability of reaching it, as if it were said: "Go out, and be upon your field," that is, settled upon it.

It is also possible that the verb "ghuduw" is construed with the meaning of "approach," as one says: "He is brought his bowl in the morning and in the evening." Al-Tibi said: a similar thing was said regarding al-Muttalib: his whip (with which he strikes) is cast upon the foolish, and his bowl upon the forbearing.

Al-harth: cleaving the earth with an iron tool or the like, so that seed or trees may be placed in it, and so that grass may be removed from it.

Al-harth is also applied to the garden, since they tend it by cultivating it to improve its trees, and this is what is meant here, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and cultivated land, forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 138] in Surat al-An'am, and it has preceded in His saying ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-takhafut: a reciprocal form from "khafata," meaning to speak secretly.

﴿Let no poor person enter it today against you﴾ is an explanation of the act of "yatakhafatun" (whispering), and "an" is explanatory, because the whispering carries the sense of speech without its letters.

The emphasis of the prohibitive verb with the emphatic nun is to add further confirmation to what they had agreed upon.

The prohibitive verb is ascribed to "miskin" (poor person) regarding the prohibition of entering, and what is meant is that some of them forbid others from letting a poor person enter their garden, that is, no one leaves a poor person to enter it. This is of the kind of kinayah (metonymy), which is common in the use of the prohibition, as in their saying: "I shall not find you doing such and such."

His saying ﴿and they went early, with a determination, as those capable﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause with the implied "qad," that is, they set out while being early-goers, capable of a determination.

The verb "ghadaw" is mentioned in the circumstantial clause for the purpose of marvelling at that ill-omened early departure, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*He spent the night, and a night was for him like the night of one with the sore, blear eye.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 17–25 (part 2 of 2):

After his saying:
*"Long has your night stretched out at al-Athmud,
and the one free of care has spent the night while you did not sleep."*

He addresses his own soul in a manner that contains an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) or two shifts.

Al-ḥard (حَرْد) is used to mean prevention, to mean strong intent, that is, haste, and to mean anger.

That is, the phrase (ʿalā ḥardin) may be linked to (qādirīna), or to the verb (ghadawā).

If it is linked to (qādirīna), then placing the complement first gives a restriction: *able to prevent*, that is, able to prevent good, or to prevent the fruit of their garden, while unable to benefit.

Expressing it as *qādirīna ʿalā ḥardin* rather than saying *wa-ghadaw ḥādirīna* is a taḥakkum (mockery). The usage of the verb of ability (qudra) is customarily mentioned with actions that are difficult for people to perform. God the Exalted says: ﴿They have no power over anything they have earned﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], and He says: ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyama: 4]. So His saying ﴿upon ḥardin, able﴾, according to this possibility, is of the type of their saying: "So-and-so owns nothing but deprivation," or "is able to achieve nothing but failure."

If ḥard is taken to mean haste and intent, then (ʿalā ḥardin) is linked to (ghadawā), explaining the kind of morning-going: that is, they went out with a morning-going of haste and eagerness. In this case (ʿalā) carries the meaning of the bāʾ of accompaniment (bā' al-musāḥaba), and the sense is: going out early with speed and vigor. And (qādirīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in (ghadawā), a ḥāl muqaddara (a clause anticipated in meaning), that is, presuming that they were able to achieve what they wanted.

In the speech there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) that they failed, indicated by His saying after it: ﴿When they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have surely gone astray"﴾ [al-Qalam: 26], and His saying before it: ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep﴾.

So they schemed against them by going early to harvest it. That is, they had no power except for anger and rage, and they were unable to do what they had intended, which was to gather the fruit of the garden.
