It is also said its meaning is: they do not make an exception by saying "if God wills," as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And do not say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] ﴿unless God wills﴾ [al-Kahf: 24]. The reason it is called an exception (istithna') is that the original form of the expression contains the particle of exception, which is "illa" (except). When someone limits himself to "in sha' Allah" without the particle of exception, that statement is called an exception, since it is by way of the presumption: "except that God wills." Moreover, since the condition returns to the meaning of exception, it is called an exception by considering the meaning and the root from which "istithna'" is derived.

On this interpretation, His saying "and they do not make an exception" is of the kind of idmaj (insertion), that is, due to the extent of their conceit in their own strength, when they resolved upon doing something they did not expect any obstacle to it. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the expression with the present verb is to bring to mind their strange condition of stinginess toward the poor and the orphans.

According to all the reports, it is known that the people of this garden were not disbelievers, so the aspect of resemblance between them and the polytheists to whom this example is struck is the ingratitude of blessing and the delusion of strength.

His saying ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord﴾: al-tawaf is walking around something from all its sides; it is said "tafa bil-Ka'bah" (he circumambulated the Ka'bah). It is intended here as a figure for the condition of striking a whole thing with the condition of one who circles a place, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿When a visitation from Satan touches them﴾ [al-A'raf: 201], and so on.

The verb (tafa) is transitive with the particle (ʿalā) by virtue of its being construed with the meaning of: "to overpower" or "to descend upon."

He did not specify the kind of the visitor, since it is evident that it is of the kind of what strikes gardens with destruction, and no purpose depends on specifying its type, because the lesson lies in what results from it. So ascribing the verb (tafa) to a visitor is like ascribing the verb in the passive voice, as if it were said: "it was circled over them while they were
asleep."

It is related from al-Farra' that the visitor is only at night, meaning that from this the dream-image which one sees in his sleep is called "tayf." It is said it is derived from "ta'ifah," which is a portion of the night. There is room for scrutiny in this.

So His saying ﴿while they were asleep﴾ is a restriction of the time of the visitor according to the first interpretation, and it is an emphasis of the meaning of "visitor" according to al-Farra's interpretation, and its benefit is depicting the condition.

The tanwin of "ta'if" is for magnification, that is, a great matter, and He has explained it by His saying ﴿So it became like the black, harvested night﴾. So it is an evil visitation. It is said: a neck of fire reached it and it was burned.

And ﴿from your Lord﴾ means coming from the side of your Lord, so "min" here is for origin, meaning that it was a punishment sent down upon them as a retribution for their failure to give thanks for the blessing.

The punishment was hastened for them before they were engaged in withholding charity, because their resolve to withhold and their mutual agreement upon it effectively established that they were withholding their charity, so they were withholding. From the verse a warning is derived for those who do not console others with their wealth.

Since the punishment of the people of this garden was worldly, there is nothing in the verse indicating that the people of the garden withheld obligatory charity.

As for al-sarim: it is said it is the night, and sarim is among the names of the night and among the names of the day, because each of them is cut off from the other, just as each of the night and the day is called "malwan," so it is said "al-malawan." On this basis, the combination of "asbahat" (it became) and "al-sarim" contains the figure of antithesis (tibaq).

It is said: al-sarim is the black ash, in the dialect of Judhaymah or Khuzaymah.

It is said: al-sarim is the name of a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing.

The choice of the word al-sarim here is due to the abundance of its meanings and the suitability of all those meanings to be intended in the verse.

Between "yasrimunnaha" and "al-sarim" there is paronomasia (jinas).

The fa' of ﴿Then they called out﴾ is for consequence upon ﴿they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning﴾, that is, when they woke in the morning they called to one another to carry out what they had plotted.

Al-tanadi: that some of them call out to others, and it implies encouragement to go out to their garden early.

Al-ghuduw: going out and leaving a place at the early part of the day, that is, its beginning.

Their saying ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾ is not a conditional clause, but it is used for urging on the slow. It is as if, due to the slowness of some of them in going out, they had turned from harvesting that day. From it is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar to al-Hajjaj at the decline of the sun on 'Arafah, urging him to hasten to the standing place: "Go early, if you want the Sunnah." And similar to this is abundant in speech.

The "ʿalā" in His saying ﴿upon your field﴾ is used to express the attainability of reaching it, as if it were said: "Go out, and be upon your field," that is, settled upon it.

It is also possible that the verb "ghuduw" is construed with the meaning of "approach," as one says: "He is brought his bowl in the morning and in the evening." Al-Tibi said: a similar thing was said regarding al-Muttalib: his whip (with which he strikes) is cast upon the foolish, and his bowl upon the forbearing.

Al-harth: cleaving the earth with an iron tool or the like, so that seed or trees may be placed in it, and so that grass may be removed from it.

Al-harth is also applied to the garden, since they tend it by cultivating it to improve its trees, and this is what is meant here, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and cultivated land, forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 138] in Surat al-An'am, and it has preceded in His saying ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-takhafut: a reciprocal form from "khafata," meaning to speak secretly.

﴿Let no poor person enter it today against you﴾ is an explanation of the act of "yatakhafatun" (whispering), and "an" is explanatory, because the whispering carries the sense of speech without its letters.

The emphasis of the prohibitive verb with the emphatic nun is to add further confirmation to what they had agreed upon.

The prohibitive verb is ascribed to "miskin" (poor person) regarding the prohibition of entering, and what is meant is that some of them forbid others from letting a poor person enter their garden, that is, no one leaves a poor person to enter it. This is of the kind of kinayah (metonymy), which is common in the use of the prohibition, as in their saying: "I shall not find you doing such and such."

His saying ﴿and they went early, with a determination, as those capable﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause with the implied "qad," that is, they set out while being early-goers, capable of a determination.

The verb "ghadaw" is mentioned in the circumstantial clause for the purpose of marvelling at that ill-omened early departure, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*He spent the night, and a night was for him like the night of one with the sore, blear eye.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 17–25 (part 2 of 2):

After his saying:
*"Long has your night stretched out at al-Athmud,
and the one free of care has spent the night while you did not sleep."*

He addresses his own soul in a manner that contains an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) or two shifts.

Al-ḥard (حَرْد) is used to mean prevention, to mean strong intent, that is, haste, and to mean anger.

In the choice of the word (ḥardin) in the verse there is one of the subtleties of i'jaz (the inimitability of the Qur'an), concerning the eloquence of the word and its refinement in meaning, and concerning how the prepositional phrase relates to it in a way that suits each of its meanings. That is, the phrase (ʿalā ḥardin) may be linked to (qādirīna), or to the verb (ghadawā).

If it is linked to (qādirīna), then placing the complement first gives a restriction: *able to prevent*, that is, able to prevent good, or to prevent the fruit of their garden, while unable to benefit.

Expressing it as *qādirīna ʿalā ḥardin* rather than saying *wa-ghadaw ḥādirīna* is a taḥakkum (mockery). The usage of the verb of ability (qudra) is customarily mentioned with actions that are difficult for people to perform. God the Exalted says: ﴿They have no power over anything they have earned﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], and He says: ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyama: 4]. So His saying ﴿upon ḥardin, able﴾, according to this possibility, is of the type of their saying: "So-and-so owns nothing but deprivation," or "is able to achieve nothing but failure."

If ḥard is taken to mean haste and intent, then (ʿalā ḥardin) is linked to (ghadawā), explaining the kind of morning-going: that is, they went out with a morning-going of haste and eagerness. In this case (ʿalā) carries the meaning of the bāʾ of accompaniment (bā' al-musāḥaba), and the sense is: going out early with speed and vigor. And (qādirīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in (ghadawā), a ḥāl muqaddara (a clause anticipated in meaning), that is, presuming that they were able to achieve what they wanted.

In the speech there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) that they failed, indicated by His saying after it: ﴿When they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have surely gone astray"﴾ [al-Qalam: 26], and His saying before it: ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep﴾.

[Page 85]

If ḥard is meant as anger and rage, it is said ḥaradun with a vowel on the rāʾ and ḥardun with the rāʾ unvowelled. The prepositional phrase is then linked to (qādirīna), and placing it first gives restriction: that is, they went out having no ability except for rage and anger against the poor, because they would break into their garden every day. So they schemed against them by going early to harvest it. That is, they had no power except for anger and rage, and they were unable to do what they had intended, which was to gather the fruit of the garden.

From al-Suddi: that *ḥardin* is the name of their village, that is, their garden. I think this is a patched-together interpretation, and it seems its author derived it from the two verbs (ughdū) and (ghadawā).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 26–32:

﴿So when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ ﴿Rather, we have been deprived.﴾ ﴿The best of them said, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify [Allah]?'"﴾ ﴿They said, "Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors.﴾ ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it. Indeed, we are turning toward our Lord [in hope]."﴾ That is, they became aware of their heedlessness, returned to themselves, and reproached themselves for their insolence and for neglecting to give thanks for the blessing that had been bestowed upon them. They knew that they had been seized because of this. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We tested them with good times and bad that they might return [to obedience]﴾ [al-A'raf: 168]. Among the wise sayings of Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah al-Iskandari is: "Whoever does not give thanks for blessings has exposed them to their removal, and whoever gives thanks for them has bound them with their tether."

The particle (lamma) indicates that its response is linked to its condition immediately and at once. The purpose of this is an allusion to the polytheists: that their situation in rectifying their affair and swiftly turning back in repentance should be like the situation of the people of this garden, who hastened to regret and asked Allah for something better in exchange.

Attributing this statement to the pronoun of ﴿the people of the garden﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] requires that they all said it together, meaning they agreed on recognizing the cause of what had befallen them.

The meaning of ﴿Indeed, we have gone astray﴾ is that they knew they had been in error, that is, away from the path of gratitude; that is, they had not been guided. This is a metonymy for the fact that what befell them was a punishment for neglecting gratitude, so "going astray" is a metaphor.

Page 86

They emphasized the statement to place themselves in the position of one who doubts that they had strayed from the path of good, because their recent heedlessness of their error was still fresh; therefore it contains an announcement of grief and remorse.

And ﴿Rather, we have been deprived﴾ is a turning away (idrab) to move on to what is more important, given the situation of their clarification, since they had plotted to deprive the poor of the surplus of their produce, so they themselves became deprived of all the fruits. Thus the greater deprivation was specifically theirs, for the deprivation of the poor is nothing in comparison with their deprivation.

The speech conveys this either through the fronting of the predicate subject (taqdim al-musnad ilayh), by bringing it as a separate pronoun, although the apparent rule would have been a concealed pronoun within the passive participle, with the pronoun implicit and placed after it, since it cannot be conceived except after hearing its referent. When the pronoun was made explicit and fronted, its fronting indicated the meaning of exclusivity, that is, restriction (qasr), and this is a relative restriction (qasr idafi). This is among the consequences of the structures and of relying on contextual indicators.

It is also possible that the going astray is literal, that is, the going astray from the path to the garden: that they said, "Indeed, we have mistaken the path in our journey to our garden," because they imagined that they had seen another garden other than the one they knew. They said this out of bewilderment about their situation.

The turning away would then be annulling (ibtali), that is, they denied that they had gone astray from the path to their garden and affirmed that they were deprived of the good of their garden. The meaning would be that it was indeed their garden, but it was destroyed, so they were deprived of its goods, in that Allah destroyed it.

And (awsatuhum) means the best of them and the nearest to good, and he was one of the three brothers. "Wasat" is used for the best of the middle: Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and He said, ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. It is also said: he is of the middle of his people (sittah qawmih), and give me from the middle of your property (sittah malik).

This statement is related without a conjunction because it is a statement in the course of dialogue, a response to their saying ﴿Rather, we have been deprived,﴾ said to them in order to make them recognize the correctness of his opinion and the flaw of their opinion. The interrogation is affirmative (taqriri), and (lawla) is a particle of urging. What is meant by (tusabbihun) is glorifying Allah, that He should not be disobeyed in His command regarding giving the zakat of their produce.

Their answer contained an admission that he had admonished them and they disobeyed him, and they indicated this by glorification at the time of their remorse for not heeding his advice. So they said, ﴿Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers,﴾ intending to answer his affirmative question with an acknowledgment of glorifying Allah, that He should not be disobeyed in His command concerning giving the rights of the poor. For among the foundations of repentance is making up what can be made up, and their acknowledgment of wronging the poor is among the foundations of repentance, because it is a report used to express regret, and glorification is the prelude to seeking forgiveness for the sin. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿So glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [an-Nasr: 3].

The sentence ﴿Indeed, we were wrongdoers﴾ is an acknowledgment of sin, and the emphasis is to establish the acknowledgment and to express concern with it. The particle (inna) with this also gives the reason for the glorification that precedes it. The object of (zalimin) is omitted so that it may encompass their wronging of themselves, by what they brought upon themselves of loss of blessing, and their wronging of the poor by withholding their right in the wealth.

The narration of their answer followed the manner of dialogue, so it was not conjoined, which is the manner we were alerted to at Allah's saying, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

When their state settled on sharing in withholding the rights of the poor, some of them began to blame others for what they had neglected, each blaming the other for what he had himself been involved in regarding this matter: from the conception of the idea of withholding from the poor what had been their right during the father's lifetime, and from supporting one another in this, and from being convinced by the resolve of the rest, and from all of them carrying out that blameworthy determination. His saying ﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other﴾ depicts this state and the mutual reproach that occurred between them with this extremely concise summary. Do you not see that the turning of some toward others depicts a situation resembling attack and rebuke, and that the form "mutual blame," with the object of the blame omitted, depicts in the hearer's mind images of some blaming others?

Each one of them received the others' blame by convicting himself of blame and including the rest with him in it, so each one of them said, ﴿Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors,﴾ to the end. This statement is therefore attributed to all of them for that reason.

So the sentence ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors"﴾ to its end may be explanatory of the sentence (yatalawamun), meaning that some blame others with this speech; it is then a report used for rebuke, in the manner of allusion to others and self-admission, together with grief and remorse expressed by what (ya waylana) conveys. That is a statement comprehensive of all blame, and the sentence was not conjoined because it is explanatory.

It is also possible that it is the reply of each one to another regarding his blame of the other. Just as they agreed in blaming one another, so too they agreed in answering one another regarding that blame, and each blamed one said to his blamer, ("Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors") and so on, as an answer confirming his blame, acknowledging the sin, hoping for pardon from Allah, and seeking compensation for their garden with something better, since He accepted their repentance and gave them the reward of this world together with the reward of the Hereafter. So the omission of the conjunction is because the verb of saying proceeds in the manner of dialogue.

Iqbal (turning toward): literally, coming to another from the direction of his face. It is derived from qubul, which is what appears of a person from the direction of his face, opposite of iqbar (turning away). Here it is a figure for the state of eagerness in blaming.

Lawm (blame): a moderate disapproval of an act or statement, below rebuke (tawbikh) and above reproach ('itab). It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6] in Surat al-Mu'minun.

Tughyan (transgression): exceeding the limit customary in arrogance and self-magnification. The meaning: "Indeed, we were transgressors" against the limits of Allah.

Then they resumed, after their remorse and repentance, hoping from Allah that He would accept their repentance, so that He would not punish them for their sin in the Hereafter or in this world, and would completely erase His punishment in this world, by compensating them for their garden, whose destruction had been decreed, with another garden better than it.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, we are turning toward our Lord [in hope]﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the sentence of hope; that is, it is a hope that includes a turning toward Him, seeking acceptance and response.

The emphasis in ﴿Indeed, we are turning toward our Lord﴾ is for the sake of concern with this orientation.

The purpose of the elaboration in their saying after the punishment had descended upon them is to instruct those for whom this parable was struck: that they have the capacity to turn back to Allah by rejecting ingratitude for His blessing, since they had associated with Him those who have no favor upon them whatsoever.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: It reached me that they sincerely repented, and Allah knew their truthfulness, so He replaced them with a garden called al-Hayawan, with grapes, where a single cluster from it is carried by a mule.

Page 89

And from Abu Khalid al-Yamani, who said: I entered that garden and saw each of its clusters like a black standing man.

The majority of readers recited ﴿an yubdilana﴾ with a sukun on the letter ba' and lightening of the dal. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far recited (yubaddilana) with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the dal, and both have the same meaning.

Ibn al-Faras said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab used this verse as evidence that whoever deliberately reduces the nisab before the year has passed, intending to flee from zakat, or mixes with another or separates after mixing, that does not cancel zakat from him, contrary to al-Shafi'i.

The basis of the inference from the verse is that the people of the garden intended, by cutting the fruits, to nullify the right of the poor, so Allah punished them by destroying their fruits.

﴿Such is the punishment. But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ This is a return to the threat against the polytheists that began with His words ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾ [al-Qalam: 17]. So the statement is a summary and conclusion of what precedes it, and it is an independent, new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i).

What is indicated by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is what the story contained of the destruction of their garden, and what they felt when they saw it in that state, along with their regret and anguish. That is, the punishment in this world will be like that which has been mentioned. So His words (kadhalika) are the predicate placed first (musnad muqaddam), and (al-'adhab) is the subject (musnad ilayhi). Placing the predicate first serves to emphasize it, to bring its image to the listener's mind.

The definiteness in (al-'adhab) is the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), and it contains an implicit reference to a mental previous knowledge (al-'ahd al-dhihni). That is, your promised punishment is like the punishment of those people, and the likeness lies in the destruction of provisions and the affliction of cutting off the fruits.

The comparison in His words ﴿Such is the punishment﴾ is not like the comparison in His words ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] and similar ones, which were discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. Rather, what is here is of the common type of comparison (al-tashbih al-muta'araf), because there exists something suitable to be the likened-to element (mushabbah bihi), namely the punishment itself, and the likened-to (mushabbah) is other than the likened-to-element (mushabbah bihi). A parallel to it is His, exalted is He, saying ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing﴾ [Hud: 102]. This differs from what is in Surat al-Baqarah, for there the likened-to-element is identical to the likened-to, for the purpose of hyperbole in bringing the likened-to to the utmost extent of the aspect of similarity in it, such that when it is intended to liken it, one resorts only to likening it to itself; so it becomes a metonymy (kinaya) for its reaching the highest levels of the aspect of similarity.

The equivalence between the likened and the likened-to is an equivalence in kind; otherwise, what they were threatened with of drought is more severe than what befell the people of the garden and longer-lasting.

His words ﴿But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾ indicate that what is meant by His words ﴿Such is the punishment﴾ is the punishment of this world.

The pronoun in ﴿if only they knew﴾ refers back to what the pronoun of the absent party in His words (We have tested them) refers to, namely the polytheists, for they used to deny the punishment of the Hereafter, so they were threatened with the punishment of this world. It cannot refer to ﴿the people of the garden﴾ [al-Qalam: 17], because they were believers in the punishment of the Hereafter and its severity.

﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) with their Lord are Gardens of Bliss.﴾ It is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because what has been mentioned of the punishment of the Hereafter for the criminals naturally gives rise to a question in the listener's mind, saying: "What is the recompense of the God-fearing?" It is a parenthetical statement (kalam mu'taridh) placed between the parts of the warning and threat, and between His saying ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾ [al-Qalam: 16] and His saying ﴿Such is the punishment﴾ [al-Qalam: 33]. The question was anticipated by His saying after it: ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35], as will come.

The fronting of the predicate (musnad) before the subject (musnad ilayhi) is for the sake of emphasis on the matter of the God-fearing, so that the mention of their great attribute precedes the mention of its reward.

The lam here is the lam of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq). "'Inda" (with) is an adverbial complement (zarf) connected to the sense of being (al-kawn) which the preposition requires. For this reason its complement was fronted together with it before the subject, for the sake of that emphasis. The fronting of the predicate with what accompanies it has produced a lengthening that arouses the listener's eagerness (tashwiq) toward the subject. The "indiyyah" (being with) here is the "indiyyah" of honour and regard.

Page 91
The idafa (annexation) of "Jannat" to "al-Na'im" indicates that they are defined by it, whereby the constant association of bliss with them is indicated; for the basic meaning of the annexation is that it is by implicit lam of entitlement, so "Jannat al-Na'im" indicates that bliss deserves them, since in their conditions there is nothing but a state of bliss for their people. Thus there is not in them what there is in the gardens of this world of hardships, such as heat at some times, or severe cold, or such as insects and wasps, or what harms like the thorns of flowers and trees, the dung of animals, and the droppings of birds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 35–36:

﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ The fa' of al-tafri' (the fa' of consequence) requires that this statement is a consequence of what precedes it: the entitlement of the God-fearing to the Gardens of Bliss, and its contrast with the threat to the polytheists of punishment in this world and the Hereafter. However, that is not explicitly stated in a way that suits this denunciation and rebuke being a consequence of it. Therefore it is necessary to posit a denial from those alluded to (the opponents), so that this consequent interrogation may be directed at them. This is what we indicated a moment ago: the anticipation or occurrence of a question.

The interrogation and what follows it of reproach, censure, and mockery at their false self-conceit indicates that what was denied them, and for which they were rebuked and deemed foolish, was a matter that had been discussed in their assemblies, or that they had ridiculed the Muslims with, in the context of denying that there would be any resurrection, and their assumption that, even on the supposition that resurrection and recompense occur, the Muslims would have no distinction or superiority at that time.

It is related from Muqatil that when the verse ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing with their Lord are Gardens of Bliss﴾ [al-Qalam: 34] was revealed, the Quraysh said: "If there is indeed a Garden of Bliss, then we shall have in it a share like our share and theirs in this world." And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that they said: "We shall be given on that day something better than what you are given," and so there was revealed His saying ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾, to the end of the verse.

The hamzah is for the interrogation of denial. The denial of equality between the Muslims and the disbelievers is made a consequence of the difference in the recompense of the two groups previously mentioned. So the denial bears upon what was said among the polytheists upon the revelation of the preceding verse, or upon the revelation of the verses before it which contrasted the reward of the believers with the reward of the polytheists, as is clearly indicated by His saying ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed, for you is what you judge﴾ [al-Qalam: 39].

The denial of placing the two groups as similar is a metonymy (kinaya) for granting the Muslims the reward of goodness in the Hereafter and depriving the polytheists of it; because the negation of equality is used in the sense of opposition between good and evil in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. Allah the Exalted said ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah: 18], and He said ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of the Garden are not equal﴾ [al-Hashr: 20], and He said ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like corrupters on earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. And al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi said:

"Ask, if you are ignorant of the people concerning us and them, for the knowing and the ignorant are not equal."

And when it is negated that the polytheists have any share in the reward of goodness, what they claimed is negated, namely that they have a better share in the Hereafter than the Muslims, just as is their situation in this world, by way of the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab).

His saying ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ is a statement addressed to the polytheists, and they are the intended referents of "the criminals". He referred to them by explicit noun rather than by a pronoun of address, because of the contrast in the description "the criminals", so that in the two descriptions there is an allusion to the cause of the negation of similarity between the two groups.

Therefore the pronoun of address in His saying ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ is not an iltifat (shift) away from the pronouns of absence in His saying ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9] and His saying ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾ [al-Qalam: 17].

The pronoun changed to the pronoun of address only in accordance with the change in the direction of the speech, because the condition of iltifat is that the pronoun changes within a single context.

"Ma lakum" is an interrogation of denial concerning the state of their judgment; "fa-ma lakum" is a mubtada' and khabar. It has already been discussed in His saying ﴿They said: "And what is for us that we should not fight in the way of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246] in Surat al-Baqarah.

And ﴿How do you judge?﴾ is a second interrogation of denial, in the position of a hal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in (lakum), meaning: nothing belongs to you in the state of your judging; i.e., if it were established for them, it would be denounced in terms of the state of their judging.

The meaning: You do not judge that you are equal to the Muslims in the reward of the Hereafter, nor that you are preferred over them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 37–38:

[Page 93]
﴿Or do you have a Book in which you study,﴾ ﴿that indeed you will have therein whatever you choose?﴾ This is an iḍrāb (a transitional turn) from rebuke to argument against their falsehood.

The interrogative implied with (am, "or") is a denial that they should have a Book, a denial based on a supposition, even though they had not claimed it.

The outcome of this transition, and of the three transitions after it, namely ﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] etc., ﴿Ask them which of them will stand surety for that﴾ [al-Qalam: 40], ﴿Or do they have partners?﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] etc., is that your judgment cannot be free of one of the following: its basis is a heavenly Book sent down from Us; or its basis is a covenant from Us that We will give you what you demand; or you have a guarantor against Us; or it is reliance on the help of your partners.

The placing of (lakum, "for you") before the subject (kitab, "a book"), which is indefinite, is because the indefiniteness is intended to express kind, so fronting the predicate became obligatory.

The pronoun in (fihi, "in it") refers to the judgment derived from His words ﴿How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36], that is, a Book concerning the judgment.

The (fi, "in") is for causality or the figurative sense of location, as you say: a book came concerning such-and-such a matter, or concerning the prohibition of such-and-such; thus (fihi) is a settled adverbial phrase serving as an attribute of (kitab). It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to (kitab), and for the prepositional phrase to be connected to the verb (tadrusun, "you study"). Deep study, through greater insight into what the Book contains, is treated as if it were an object contained within the Book, as you say: we have a lesson in the book of Sibawayh.

In this there is an incidental allusion (idmaj bi-l-ta'rid) that they are unlettered and not people of a Book, and that when a Book came to them for their guidance and to join them to the nations possessing Books, they denied its blessing and rejected it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your mention; will you not reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10], and He says: ﴿Or you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Indeed there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 157].

The clause ﴿that indeed you will have therein whatever you choose﴾ is in the position of the object of (tadrusun), on the basis that its wording is quoted,

[Page 94]
i.e., you study this expression, just as Allah the Exalted's words ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ [al-Saffat: 78] ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat: 79] (are a quotation), i.e., you study the clause ﴿that indeed you will have therein whatever you choose﴾.
The (fihi) would then be a verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi) for its counterpart in His words ﴿fihi tadrusun﴾, its repetition intended to add further connection of the clause to the preceding one, just as the word (min) is repeated in His words ﴿And from the fruits of the palm and grapes you take from them an intoxicant﴾ [al-Nahl: 67], whose underlying form is: you take an intoxicant.

(Takhayyarun, "you choose") originally was tatakhayyarun with two tas, one of which was deleted for lightness. Takhayyur (choosing) is the seeking of what is good, i.e., seeking what is more excellent. The meaning: indeed in that Book there is for you what you choose of the best reward.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 39:

﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, binding until the Day of Resurrection, that indeed you shall have whatever you decide?﴾

(Am) is used to shift to another proof, namely the negation that the basis of their claim is a covenant they took upon Allah for themselves, that He would treat them on the Day of Resurrection according to what they judge for themselves. Thus the interrogation that must be presumed after (am) is denunciatory, and (bāligha) is an emphasis. The original meaning of bāligha is "reaching what is sought through it," and this is a metaphor for "severe, emphatic," being likened to a thing that has reached the end of its course. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: To Allah belongs the conclusive proof﴾ [al-An'am: 149].

His saying (ʿalaynā) is a second attribute of (aymān), meaning: We have sworn them to you to establish your right over us.

And ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a third attribute of (aymān), meaning: oaths that are perpetual, from which there is no release. From the two attributes it results that they are covenants that are emphatic and continuous throughout the length of time. The Day of Resurrection is therefore not the endpoint of acting upon those oaths; rather it is an explicit statement of perpetuity, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 5] in Surah al-Ahqaf.

The phrase "until the Day of Resurrection" is connected to the stability implied in the predicate in His saying ﴿you have oaths﴾, and it is not good for it to be connected to (bāligha) as a connection of a loose adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf al-laghw), because that would make (bāligha) used in a well-known, near-literal meaning, whereas the metaphor we mentioned is more eloquent. The clause ﴿that indeed you shall have whatever you decide﴾ is an explanation of (aymān), meaning: oaths with this wording.

The meaning of mā taḥkumūn is "what you order without consultation." It is said: "They descended to the judgment of so-and-so" (nazalū ʿalā ḥukm fulān), meaning they did not specify a particular demand, but entrusted the determination of their right to so-and-so. Khaṭṭāb or Ḥiṭṭān ibn al-Muʿallā said:

The times have brought me down to his judgment, from a lofty, towering height to a low place.

That is, without my choice or any action of mine; it is as if I made fate the judge, and it brought me down from my strongholds and disposed of me as it willed.

Among their well-known sayings that became proverbs is "ḥukmuka musammaṭan" (pronounced with a dammah on the mīm, a fatḥah on the sīn, and a fatḥah on the second mīm, doubled), meaning: your judgment is yours, executed without any objection against you in it.

And Ibn ʿUthma said:

To you belong the quarter-share of the spoils and the choice portions, and your judgment, and the eager gifts and the surplus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 40:

﴿Ask them, which of them will guarantee that?﴾ This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) of the sentence ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, binding until the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39], because oaths, which are covenants (al-'uhud), ordinarily require guarantors (al-kufala'), as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Remember the alliance of Dhu al-Majaz, in which covenants were made and guarantors were put forward."

When the denial that they possess covenants was mentioned, it was completed by asking them to specify who among them are the guarantors (al-zu'ama') of those oaths.

Thus the interrogative in His words (Ask them, which of them will guarantee that?) is used in the sense of mockery (al-tahakkum), in addition to the rebuke directed at them.

Al-za'im (the guarantor) is the surety (al-kafil). The guarantor has been made one of them as an added element of mockery, namely that He made the guarantor for them one of their own, on account of their arrogance and their presumption toward the majesty of God Most High.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 41:

﴿Or do they have associates? Then let them bring their associates, if they are truthful.﴾

Page 96

(Am) is a third transitional "idrab" (a shift from one topic to another, here meaning a turn away from the previous argument) to refuting another basis assumed for them in the grounds of their saying: "We will be given what the Muslims are given, or something better than what they are given." This is to assume that their idols will help them and will grant them a share of the reward of good in the Hereafter.

The meaning is: rather, has it established for them, that is, for their sake and benefit, associates, that is, associates with us in divinity according to their claim. So the object of "shurakaʾ" (associates) is omitted because it is well known to them, and "shurakaʾ" becomes like a title. That is, "Or do their gods belong to them? Then let them bring them so that they may benefit them on the Day of Resurrection."

The "lam" in "lahum" (for them) is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajl), that is, for their sake, with an implied noun: for the sake of their support. So the lam is like the lam in the saying of Abu Sufyan on the day of Uhud: "We have al-ʿUzzā, and you have no ʿUzzā."

The indefiniteness of "shurakaʾ" within the scope of the interrogative used for denial indicates the negation that any of the associates, that is, the idols, belong to them, that is, for their benefit. It thus includes the idols of all Arab tribes, both those whose worship was shared among the tribes and those specific to certain tribes.

The style of speech has been shifted from address to third-person absence because it follows (﴿Ask them which of them will stand surety for that﴾ [al-Qalam: 40]). The most fitting person to know the truth of this refutation is the Prophet (ﷺ), and this entails directing this refutation to them by way of allusion (taʿrid).

The branching ("tafri'") in His words ﴿then let them bring their associates﴾ is a branching upon the negation that their gods can benefit them, so it is determined that the command "fa-l-yaʾtū" (then let them bring) is a command of challenge (amr taʿjīz).

The attribution of "shurakaʾ" (associates) to their pronoun in His words ﴿then let them bring their associates﴾ is to refute the attribute of partnership in divinity from them, that is, they are not associates in divinity except according to these people, for true divinity is not relative to a group or tribe.

Similar unrestricted usage is frequent in the Qur'an, including His words ﴿Say: Call upon your associates, then plot against me, and give me no respite﴾ [al-A'raf: 195].

[Page 97]

It is permissible that ﴿on the day when the shin is uncovered﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿then let them bring their associates﴾ [al-Qalam: 41], meaning: let them bring those they claimed (as partners) on the Day of Resurrection. This is a graceful transition (husn al-takhallus) to mention the terrors of the Resurrection upon them.

It is also permissible that it is a new sentence (istinaf) connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: Remember the day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, etc., as a reminder of the terrors of that day.

On both possibilities regarding the connection of ﴿yawma﴾ (the day), the intended day is the Day of Resurrection.

Uncovering the shin (al-kashf 'an saq) is a metaphor (mathal) for the severity of the state, the hardship of the matter, and the terror. Its origin is that when a person is panicked, he hastens in walking and gathers up his garments, so that he uncovers his shin, as it is said: "Roll up your sleeves for serious work." Also, in times of panic and defeat, free women would gather up their shins in flight or in work, so their shins would be exposed, the terror of the matter preoccupying them from guarding against showing what they would ordinarily not show. So it is said: "She uncovered her shin," or "she rolled up her shin," or "she showed her shin." 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

How can I sleep on my bed, when a fierce raid has overtaken Syria?
It distracts the elder from his sons, and exposes ***
the servants of the chaste, virgin maiden.

In the hadith of the Battle of Uhud, Anas ibn Malik said: "The people fled from the Prophet ﷺ, and I saw 'A'isha and Umm Sulaym, and indeed they were both rolling up their garments; I could see the anklets of their shins, carrying waterskins on their backs, then pouring them into the mouths of the people, then returning and filling them again," etc.

So when they say: "A man uncovered his shin," it is a metonymy (kinaya) for a terror that befell him, even if he did not uncover his shin. And when they say: "The matter uncovered its shin," they have likened it to a terrified woman. Likewise, "War uncovered its shin"; all of this is figurative, since there is no shin there. Hatim said:

A young man of war: if war bites him, he bites it back,
and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up as well.

And the grandfather of Tarafa from the Hamasa said:

It uncovered its shin for them,
and the evil of the fight appeared, bare.

Ibn 'Abbas recited ﴿yawma takshifu﴾ with a feminine (taʼ) prefix and in the active voice, on the estimate that the hardship uncovers its shin, or the Resurrection uncovers it. Close to this is their saying: "War stood upon a shin."

The meaning is: the day when the states of the people reach the extreme of severity and terror. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Uncovered of a shin: of distress and severity, and it is the most severe hour on the Day of Resurrection."

'Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he was asked about this, and he said: "If something of the Qur'an is obscure to you, seek it in poetry, for it is the register (diwan) of the Arabs. Have you not heard the poet's saying:

So it is said: "She uncovered her shin," or "she rolled up her shin," or "she showed her shin." 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

How can I sleep on my bed, when a fierce raid has overtaken Syria?
It distracts the elder from his sons, and exposes ***

A young man of war: if war bites him, he bites it back,
and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up as well.

And the grandfather of Tarafa from the Hamasa said:

It uncovered its shin for them,
and the evil of the fight appeared, bare.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 44–45:

Page 100
﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them step by step from where they do not know.﴾ ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ The fa' (فاء) here marks the consequence of the speech that it conjoins to the speech preceding it, because the first speech was the cause of what follows it. After the aim of admonishing and warning them and exposing the falsity of their illusions had been fulfilled, this interjection was appended as consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), that Allah has undertaken to exact retribution from the deniers and to grant him victory over them.

His saying ﴿So leave Me with those who deny﴾ and the like conveys an image of the state of the object of (ذَرْ, dhar, "leave") in that he is entrusted to be sufficed in the burden of something without seeking help from the one bearing the burden. It is like the state of one who sees the addressee has begun to avenge himself and sees that he will not reach by that the level of the object of (ذَرْ), because He is more capable than the one wronged of exacting retribution from the wrongdoer; so he leaves it to Him and does not ask the rightful owner for help in taking his right. For this reason, a verb indicating a request to abandon is used, and after it an object of accompaniment is given. From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]. Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unuf, concerning His saying (﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]): In it is a threat and warning, meaning, leave me and him, and you will see what I do. It is a phrase said by one who is enraged when his anger and fury intensify and he dislikes to intercede for the one who has angered him. So the meaning of the speech is: there is no intercession for this disbeliever.

The waw (واو) is the waw of accompaniment (واو المعية), and what follows it is an object of accompaniment (مفعول معه). It is not valid for the waw to be conjunctive, because the intended meaning is: leave Me with them.

The word ḥadīth (حديث) may be intended to refer to the Qur'an, and it is called ḥadīth because of what it contains of reports about Allah, the Exalted, and reports of past nations and reports of unseen matters. It has been named thus in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] in Surah al-A'raf, and His saying ﴿Is it at this statement that you wonder?﴾ [al-Najm: 59] ﴿and laugh?﴾ [al-Najm: 60], the verse in Surah al-Najm, and His saying ﴿Is it then at this statement that you are complacent?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] in Surah al-Waqi'ah.

The demonstrative (اسم الإشارة) on this view points to something present in the mind from what of the Qur'an had been revealed earlier.

It is also possible that by ḥadīth is meant the report about the Resurrection, which is what His saying comprises: ﴿On the Day when the shin will be uncovered﴾ [al-Qalam: 42], the verse.

Page 101
The demonstrative then refers to that speech, and the meaning is: it suffices for striking them that you entrust their affair to Me; I know how to exact retribution from them, so do not occupy yourself with them and rely upon Me.
This includes an allusive threat to the deniers, because they hear this speech.

This is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) of victory and a threat to them of retribution in this world, because it is a hastening for the consolation of the Messenger.

The clause ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ is an explanation of the content of ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾, in terms of the fact that istidraj and imla' are followed by retribution. It is as if He said: We will seize them for their deeds, so do not be impatient for the retribution, for its occurrence is certain, but it is deferred for a wisdom that requires its deferment.

Istidraj (الاستدراج) is drawing something down from one degree to another, like a ladder. The original sense of the sin and ta' in it is for seeking, i.e., attempting to proceed by degrees, that is, moving through the steps, and the context indicates the intended sense of descent, since moving through steps occurs both upward and downward. Then its use became common for a good treatment of one who does evil, up to a determined term at whose arrival his punishment comes. The meaning of ﴿from where they do not know﴾ is that their istidraj, which leads to the arrival of punishment upon them, comes to them from circumstances and causes which they do not perceive as leading them to destruction, and this is more conducive to the intensity of their regret when calamities befall them. So (مِن) is for the starting point, and (حيث) is for the figurative place, i.e., the causes, actions and states which they suppose bring them good, but which are revealed to them as harm. The object of (لا يعلمون) is a pronoun omitted, referring back to (حيث).

Umlī (أملي) is the present tense of amlā, in its shortened form, meaning to grant respite and delay. It is derived from al-mala (الملا), shortened, which is a period and a time; from it is said al-malawān (الملوان) for night and day. So amlā means to lengthen in time, and its verbal noun is imlā'.

The lam in (لهم) is the lam called lam al-tabyin (لام التبيين), which clarifies the connection of its governed noun to its governing element because of some obscurity in it, for the derivation of the verb amlā from al-malw, meaning time, is a derivation that is not clear because the sense of the event is obscure in it.

The nūn in ﴿We will lead them step by step﴾ is the nūn of the speaker who is joined with others (نون المتكلم المشارك), and what is intended is Allah and His angels entrusted with subjecting existents and linking the states of some to others in a manner by which Allah's will is accomplished. Therefore the nūn of the plural speaker was used. Thus istidraj is a immediate connection to Allah's power, so it occurs through the mediation of the angels entrusted with it, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], the verse.

As for imla', it is Allah's knowledge of the postponement of their seizure. The connection of knowledge is exclusive to Allah, so the singular pronoun was used with it. In this variation of the two pronouns there is an artistic variety (تفنن).

A parallel to this verse is His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 182], ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf: 183], in terms of the fact that both are a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) of victory and a reassurance to him that the continuance of the disbelievers in blessing is only istidraj and imla' and a blow resembling a plot, and that Allah is accomplishing His command concerning them. This is like His saying: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196], ﴿a brief enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197].

The position of (إنّ) is that of causation and explanation, as previously mentioned at His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The application of the word kayd (كيد, plot) to Allah's bestowal of favour upon a people while intending harm to them is a figurative usage, because it resembles the act of the plotter in that good is hastened and followed by evil.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 46:

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾ This is another turn (idrab) moving to yet another refutation of their excuses for turning away from responding to the call of the Prophet ﷺ, which began with His saying ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a Book?﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿Or do you have oaths?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Or do they have partners?﴾ [al-Qalam: 41]. For after He negated that they had any proof supporting the soundness of their condition, or any promise to give them what they desire, or any allies to support them, He turned the speech to negating that there could be any harm upon them in responding to the call of Islam. This is a thorough exhaustion of every excuse that might be conceived, on the supposition that the Messenger ﷺ had asked them for a wage for his guidance to them, so that the heaviness of the financial burden on their souls prevented them from answering him.

The interrogative implied by (am) is an interrogative of denial, rejecting the assumption that such a thing could occur to their minds, an assumption that is required by the inductive examination of their intentions from their manner of turning toward the call to goodness and right guidance.

Al-maghram (debt, financial burden): what is imposed on a person to pay from his wealth without any exchange or any offence.

Al-muthqal: one upon whom a heavy thing has been laid. Here it is a metaphor for being apprehensive (ishfaq).

The fa' (fa) is for sequence and causation: meaning, as a consequence of that, you have burdened them, so that this becomes an excuse from them for not accepting what you call them to.

﴿Min maghram﴾ is connected to (muthqalun). The (min) is ibtida'iyyah (denoting origin), and it is a figurative origin in the sense of causation. The fronting of the object before its governing verb is for emphasis on the cause of the hardship before mentioning it, along with observance of the verse-ending (fasilah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verse 47:

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ This is another turn (idrab) by which he moved from the stages of refuting fabricated excuses, which they could hold on to as a pretext for turning away from accepting the call of the Qur'an, cutting off what they might invent of excuses by way of induction (istiqra') and the prevention of any gap (man' al-khuluw).

The preceding refutations dealt with excuses imagined for them that were based on things observed (mushahadat). Now the discourse moves to a refutation of a different kind: the refutation of an imagined argument in which they rely on knowing some of the matters hidden from people (al-mughayyabat). These are among the things that God has reserved for His own knowledge, and it is what is expressed by "the unseen (al-ghayb)," as was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is firmly established among all people that the matters of the unseen are known only to God, or to whomever of His servants He informs of some of them.

The speech here involves an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "Do they have the knowledge of the unseen?" as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35] in Surat al-Najm.

Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿Do they have the unseen﴾ is that it has come into their knowledge and capacity, either through all of them having access to it, or through their great men conveying it to them and them receiving it from them.

The fronting of ("with them", 'indahum) before the subject, which is definite, serves to express exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: the knowledge of the unseen has become theirs, not God's.

The meaning of "they write" (yaktubun) is: they stipulate and determine, as in His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], and His saying ﴿the decree of God upon you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. That is, they stipulate for themselves that happiness lies in turning away from the call of Islam, and they impose this upon the common mass of their followers.

The clause ﴿so they write it down﴾ follows as a consequence of the clause ﴿Or do they have the unseen﴾, on the basis that what is in the unseen is supposed to be a witness to their judgment for themselves, referred to by His saying ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36], as you have understood a moment ago.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 68, verses 48–50:

﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressed (in distress).﴾ ﴿Had he not been overtaken by a favor from his Lord, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of what preceded: the refutation of the claims and slanders of the polytheists against the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ), and what followed from it, namely God's guarantee to His Messenger (ﷺ) of the final outcome of victory. The reason is that his (the Prophet's ﷺ) intense grief over them could bring despair into his soul regarding the attainment of his desire and the success of his effort. So He (God) made a consequence of it the strengthening of him, the urging him to perseverance, and the continuation of his adherence to guidance. He also informed him that such steadfastness raises his rank in the station of prophethood, so that he would be among the possessors of resolve (ulu al-'azm). So He reminded him with the example of Yunus (peace be upon him), when he hastened ahead of his Lord's command; God disciplined him, then chose him, relented toward him, and made him among the righteous, as a reminder intended to be a warning.

By "the decree of your Lord" here is meant His command, namely what He charged him with of sending (as a Messenger) and of undertaking the burdens of the call. This decree is what is inferred from the verses on the command to call (to the faith), the first of which is ﴿O you wrapped in your cloak﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 2], up to His saying ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 7]. So this is the patience commanded in this verse too. Undoubtedly, patience for this requires awaiting the promise of victory and not being impatient at its delay until its appointed term in God's knowledge.

"The companion of the fish" is Yunus ibn Matta, whose mention was already given when He said ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾ [al-An'am: 84] up to ﴿and Yunus﴾ [al-An'am: 86] in Surat al-An'am.

The "companion" (sahib) is one who accompanies another, i.e., is with him in some or most circumstances. Its application to Yunus is because the fish swallowed him, then cast him out, so "the companion of the fish" became a title for him, because that state was a strong association (ma'iyyah).

Yunus's reproach was for his impatience with the denial of his people, who were the people of Nineveh, as was mentioned in Surat as-Saffat.

(Idh) is a temporal adverb, and it with its clause is connected to a stationed (implied) predicate in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: in the state of the time of his calling upon his Lord. For he called upon his Lord only to be rescued from his distress, which befell him because of his anger and his impatience with his people. That is: let there not come from you what would compel you to a calling like his.

Al-makzum: the confined, the enclosed. It is said: "kazama al-bab" (he closed the door), and "kazama al-nahr" when he dammed the river. The meaning: he called out in a state of confinement in the belly of the fish.

This state is expressed by a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) because it indicates permanence: he is in a confinement for which release is not expected for one like him. This is a preparation for the favor of rescue from such confinement.

His saying ﴿Had he not been overtaken by a favor from his Lord, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland﴾ etc. is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the implication of the prohibition in His saying ﴿and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out﴾ etc., because it includes a warning against falling into a distress of the kind of Yunus's distress, without knowing how its relief would come.

(An) may be a lightened form of (anna), its noun being an omitted pronoun of matter (damir sha'n), and the clause ﴿overtaken by a favor from his Lord﴾ is its predicate. It may also be a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning: had there not been an overtaking by a mercy from his Lord.

Tadarruk: a reciprocal form from "dark" (with fatha/ harakah), which is catching up, i.e., that some travelers catch up with others, and it implies their racing. Here it is used for the intensification of God's favor reaching him.

Nabdh: throwing and abandoning. Al-'ara' (with madd): the open expanse of land with no vegetation and no building.

The meaning: the fish or the sea would have thrown him onto the empty open land, because the fish that swallowed him is of the kind that suckles its young, so it approaches empty, far-reaching shores out of fear for itself and its offspring.

The meaning: God bestowed a favor upon him by causing a gourd plant (shajarat al-yaqtin) to grow over him, as in Surat as-Saffat.

Included in this is the excellence of repentance and humble supplication to God, and that had it not been for his repentance and his supplication to God and God's bestowing upon him favor after favor, the fish would have expelled him from its belly dead, and the waves would have thrown him onto the shore, so he would have been a disfigured spectacle for onlookers; or alive, cast out in the open wasteland without finding relief; or he would have escaped after hardship while God was angry with him, so he would be blameworthy (mazmum) before God, disapproved of by Him. These are many favors upon him, since He rescued him from all these predicaments with a rescue that broke the normal course.

This meaning is folded up in an admirable manner and indicated in an eloquent way by the sentence ﴿Had he not been overtaken by a favor from his Lord, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy﴾.

The method of the exegetes in unfolding this folded meaning is that the clause ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and that this circumstance is a restriction on the answer of (lawla), so the sense of the speech is: Had he not been overtaken by a favor from his Lord, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland in a blameworthy manner; that is, but Yunus was cast out onto the open wasteland not blameworthy.

What led them to this interpretation is that his being cast out onto the open wasteland is an actual occurrence, so it cannot be the answer of the condition, because (lawla) requires the non-occurrence of its answer due to the existence of its condition; so the answer cannot be something that has occurred, and it was therefore necessary to take the answer as restricted by the circumstantial clause, that is, his blame was negated at the time of his being cast onto the open wasteland.

It appears to me in the detailed structure of the composition another possibility: that the answer of (lawla) is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿while he was suppressed﴾, together with what the nominal sentence structure conveys of the firmness of the suppression, as you have just learned. So if that state had continued, his being cast onto the open wasteland would not have occurred, and the conditional with (lawla) would be attached to the clause ﴿when he called out while he was suppressed﴾, meaning: he would have remained suppressed, that is, confined in the belly of the fish forever. This is the meaning of His saying in Surat as-Saffat ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify (God), he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [as-Saffat: 143–144]. And the clause ﴿he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy﴾ is made an explanatory resumption arising from the ambiguity produced by the position of (lawla).

The lam in it is the lam of oath, for confirmation, because it breaks the normal course, so its emphasis removes the possibility of metaphor. The meaning: indeed he was cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy. The blameworthy (mazmum) either means the sinner, because sin entails blame in this world and punishment in the next; this is the meaning of His saying in the verse of as-Saffat ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [as-Saffat: 142]; or it means defective, namely being naked and hungry, so it corresponds to His saying ﴿Then We cast him onto the open wasteland while he was sick﴾ [as-Saffat: 145], for sickness is also a defect.

The indefinite form of (ni'mah) is for magnification, because it is a multiplied and repeated favor.

Following from this negation is the report that God chose him and made him among the righteous.

The "righteous" (al-salihin) here means the preferred among the prophets. Abraham (peace be upon him) said ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 83], and this is an allusion to the fact that righteousness is the root of goodness and the raising of ranks. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants﴾ [at-Tahrim: 10] in Surat at-Tahrim.

Ibn 'Abbas said: God returned revelation to Yunus and interceded for him regarding himself and his people.

Abraham (peace be upon him) said ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 83], and this is an allusion to the fact that righteousness is the root of goodness and the raising of ranks. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants﴾ [at-Tahrim: 10] in Surat at-Tahrim.

Ibn 'Abbas said: God returned revelation to Yunus and interceded for him regarding himself and his people.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 68, verses 51–52:**

﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad."﴾ ﴿But it is not except a Reminder to the worlds.﴾

This is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿Leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44]. Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of some of what the souls of the polytheists harbour towards the Prophet ﷺ of spite, rage, and concealed evil when they hear the Qur'an.

*Al-zalaq* (the slip): with two fatḥahs, it is the slipping of the foot due to the smoothness of the ground, from mud upon it or oil. It was mentioned in His saying ﴿and it becomes a smooth, slippery ground﴾ [al-Kahf: 40] in Surah al-Kahf.

Since slipping generally leads to falling, *al-zalaq* and what is derived from it were used, by way of metonymy (*kinayah*), for falling and being overthrown. From this is His saying here ﴿would almost make you slip﴾, meaning they would cause you to fall and throw you down.

It is narrated from Mujahid: that they would pierce you with their gaze. Al-Qurtubi said: it is said *zalaqa al-sahm wa zahaqa* (the arrow slipped and passed through) when it passes through. I have not seen this from anyone else. Al-Raghib said, quoting Yunus: "*al-zalaq* and *al-izlaq* have not been heard except in the Qur'an."

Page 108

I say: In all of these interpretations, the causing to slip by their eyes is an implicit metaphor (*istiʿarah makniyyah*): the glances were likened to arrows, and the thing likened to (the arrows) was alluded to by something belonging to it, which is the verb (*yuzliqunaka*, "they would make you slip"). This is like His saying ﴿Satan only caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ [Al ʿImran: 155].

Nafiʿ and Abu Jaʿfar read *yazliqunaka* with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, the present tense of *zalaqa* with a fatḥah on the lām, meaning *yazlaqu* transitively, "when he removes him from his place." The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ.

The present form *yakādu* ("would almost") is used to indicate the continuation of that in the future. The past form *samiʿū* ("they heard") occurs with *lammā* ("when") and indicates that it has actually taken place from them, and is not merely a supposition.

The *lām* in *layuzliqūnaka* is the *lām al-ibtidāʾ* (the emphatic lām), which often enters the predicate of an *inna* (indeed) with a kasrah; it also distinguishes the light (*mukhaffafah*) *in* from the negating *in* (*al-nāfiyah*).

The pronoun in *innahu la-majnūn* ("indeed he is mad") refers to the Prophet ﷺ, as a quotation of their speech among themselves. So the referent of the pronoun is within the speech of some of them; or there is no referent for the pronoun in their speech, because it is directed to the one they usually talk about in most of their gatherings.

The meaning: they say this as an excuse for themselves, since they found in the Reminder they heard no opening for criticising it. So they turned to criticising its bearer ﷺ, saying he is mad, in order to move from that to the claim that the speech flowing from his tongue cannot be trusted, and to divert their common people from listening to it. Therefore Allah refuted their saying "he is mad" with His saying ﴿But it is not except a Reminder to the worlds﴾, meaning: the Qur'an is nothing but a Reminder to all people, and it is not the speech of madmen. From this it moves on to the point that the one who recites it is not mad in any way.

*Al-dhikr* (the Reminder): the reminding of Allah. Speech (*al-kalām*) is the noblest type of speech, because in it lies the welfare of people.

The pronoun in *huwa* ("it") refers not to something previously mentioned but to something known from the context, and the indication of the context returns each of the two third-person pronouns to its referent, as in the saying of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas:

*We returned, and had it not been for us, their multitude would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have seized what they had gathered.*

That is: the unbelievers would have seized what the Muslims had gathered.

In His saying ﴿and they say, "Indeed, he is mad"﴾ together with His saying at the beginning of the surah ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2], there is a fine device of returning the end to the beginning (*radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr*).

So when it is established that the Qur'an is a Reminder, it becomes invalid for its conveyor to be mad. **Surah al-Haqqah**

It was named "Surah al-Haqqah" in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "One day I went out in Mecca, seeking to confront the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before I embraced Islam. I found that he had preceded me to the Sacred Mosque, so I stood behind him. He began Surah al-Haqqah, and I began to marvel at the composition of the Qur'an. I said to myself, 'By Allah, this is a poet!' He then recited ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41]. I said, 'A soothsayer!' He then recited ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Haqqah: 43], up to the end of the surah. Then Islam entered my heart in every place."

It is titled "al-Haqqah" in the mushafs, in the books of Sunnah, and in the books of tafsir. Al-Firuzabadi said in *Basair Dhawi al-Tamyiz*: it is also called "Surat al-Silsilah" (the Surah of the Chain), because of His saying ﴿then in a chain﴾ [al-Haqqah: 32]. Al-Jaʿbari, in his poem on the order of the revelation of the surahs, named it "al-Waʿiyah" (the Receptive one), and perhaps he took this from the occurrence of His saying ﴿and a receptive ear will receive it﴾ [al-Haqqah: 12]. I have not seen any predecessor for him in this naming.

Page 111

The reason for its name "Surat al-Haqqah" is that this word occurs at its beginning, and it does not occur at the beginning of any other surah of the Qur'an.

It is Meccan by consensus. The implication of the aforementioned report from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab is that it was revealed in the fifth year before the Hijrah, since ʿUmar embraced Islam after the emigration of the Emigrants to Abyssinia, and the emigration to Abyssinia took place in the fifth year before the Hijrah to Medina.

This surah is counted as the seventy-seventh in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surah Tabarak and before Surah al-Maʿarij.

The counters from the major cities agree that its verses number fifty-one.

* * *

**Its purposes:**

This surah contains the awe-inspiring depiction of the Day of Resurrection, and the warning to those who deny it of its occurrence. It also reminds them of what befell the nations that denied it, of punishment in this world and then the punishment of the Hereafter, and it warns those who deny the messengers of Allah by means of the nations that associated partners with Allah and denied.

Incorporated into this is that Allah saved the believers from the punishment, and in that is a reminder of Allah's blessing upon mankind, in that He preserved their kind by saving them from the Flood.

It also describes the terrors of the recompense and the differences among people on that day, describes the horror of the state of punishment for disbelief and for rejecting the law of Islam, extols the Qur'an, declares the Messenger ﷺ free of being other than a messenger, declares Allah exalted above allowing one who fabricates against Him to remain, strengthens the Messenger ﷺ, and warns the polytheists of the fulfilment of the threat contained in the Qur'an.
